title: King Casimir grants Jews legal protections in Poland
summary: Amid the Black Death scapegoating across Western Europe, King Casimir the Great of Poland granted Jews legal protections, inviting them to settle towns and run economic affairs.

citation.quote: In the mid-1300s, as the Black Death burned across Western Europe, Jews became scapegoats, booted from one fiefdom to the next, until the Kingdom of Poland saw an opportunity for economic development: in 1343, King Casimir the Great granted Jews legal protections.

title: Partition of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth
summary: Prussian, Russian, and Austrian troops simultaneously invaded the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and divided it among themselves, placing Sam's ancestors under Russian rule.

citation.quote: Centuries passed, times of strife and times of acceptance, until this world shattered in 1772. That August, Prussian, Russian, and Austrian troops simultaneously invaded the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and sliced it up amongst themselves.

title: Tsar Alexander II takes the throne
summary: Alexander II emerged as Russia's tsar, presenting himself as a bearer of modernity who would later ease antisemitic laws and free the serfs.

citation.quote: Out of this morass, Tsar Alexander II emerged in 1855 as a bearer of modernity.

title: Alexander II frees Russia's serfs
summary: Tsar Alexander II emancipated Russia's serfs, though the freed serfs were forced to pay back the costs of their emancipation. He also eased some antisemitic laws.

citation.quote: He freed Russia's serfs in 1861 (forcing them to pay back the costs incurred by their emancipation) and eased some of the old antisemitic laws, including the university quotas and the childhood military conscription.

title: Birth of Pati Kremer
summary: Pati Kremer, who would help found the Bund and translate Marx into Yiddish, was born in Vilna.

citation.quote: Pati Kremer was born in 1867 in Vilna. She has fought for the workers since she was fifteen, when she tried to teach ungrateful seamstresses how to read in Novgorod.

title: Germany frees Jews of last legal restrictions
summary: Germany freed Jews of their last legal restrictions, following the assimilationist efforts of figures like Moses Mendelssohn and Rahel Varnhagen.

citation.quote: In Germany, Jews like the philosopher Moses Mendelssohn and the saloniste Rahel Varnhagen sought to slay Christian prejudice through urbane intellect, social glitter, and commercial triumph. Germany freed Jews of their last legal restrictions in 1871.

title: First Jewish workers' strikes in Vilna
summary: The first strikes broke out in Vilna among teenage girls who rolled cigarettes and sewed socks in the city's factories, foreshadowing a wider trade union movement among Jewish workers.

citation.quote: The first strikes broke out in 1871 among the teenage girls who rolled cigarettes and sewed socks in the city's factories.

title: Narodniks go to the countryside
summary: Jewish and Christian Narodniks, romantic socialists who believed in the redemptive power of the peasantry, left the cities for the countryside to incite a peasant uprising, but were promptly reported to police.

citation.quote: In 1874, Jewish and Christian Narodniks abandoned the cities for the countryside, where these mostly middle-class kids imagined they could incite a peasant uprising. The peasants promptly reported them to the police.

title: Vladimir Medem born in Minsk
summary: Vladimir Medem was born in Minsk to an army-doctor father who converted to Lutheranism and had his son baptized to spare him anti-Jewish laws.

citation.quote: He was born in 1879 in Minsk, where his father, an army doctor who converted to Lutheranism to keep his job, had him baptized to spare him the indignities of anti-Jewish laws.

title: Execution of Perovskaya and conspirators; Helfman dies
summary: The government sentenced Perovskaya and five accomplices to hang. Hesya Helfman, the Jewish seamstress who ran the safe house, died of blood poisoning in the Peter and Paul Fortress after giving birth.

citation.quote: The government sentenced Perovskaya to hang, along with her five accomplices. One of them was Hesya Helfman, a beautiful Jewish seamstress who had fled an arranged marriage for Kyiv's revolutionary underground, then run the safe house where Perovskaya and her co-conspirators plotted the tsar's assassination.

title: Pogroms sweep the Pale; Pinsker advances proto-Zionism
summary: Pogroms swept the Pale of Settlement following Alexander II's murder, hitting Jews regardless of class or politics. In the aftermath, Odesa physician Leon Pinsker advanced the idea that Jews could only be safe in an independent state.

citation.quote: In the aftermath of the 1881 pogroms, an Odesa physician named Leon Pinsker began to advance the new idea that Jews could only be safe in an independent Jewish state. In a few years, this would be known as Zionism.

title: Marx mocks Geneva-based Russian exiles in letter to Engels
summary: In an 1881 letter to Friedrich Engels, the elderly Marx sneered at the luxury enjoyed by Russian exiles who had come to Geneva to carry on propaganda in Russia.

citation.quote: In an 1881 letter to Friedrich Engels, the elderly Marx sneered at the luxury exiles had who "in order to carry on propaganda in Russia…came to Geneva!"

title: Assassination of Tsar Alexander II
summary: Sophia Perovskaya masterminded the bombing of Tsar Alexander II's carriage in Saint Petersburg. A second bomb thrown after the tsar emerged killed both the assassin and the monarch.

citation.quote: In 1881, the aristocratic Sophia Perovskaya did Zasulich one better and masterminded the death of Tsar Alexander II.

title: May Laws restore antisemitic restrictions
summary: Tsar Alexander III brought back the old antisemitic laws his father had overturned. The May Laws set off the first great Jewish exodus from the Russian Empire toward Antwerp and overseas destinations.

citation.quote: In 1882, the new tsar brought back the old antisemitic laws that his father had overturned. These May Laws set off the first great Jewish exodus from the empire.

title: Police roundups follow Alexander II assassination
summary: Educated radicals like Mikhael Zametkin and Abraham Cahan fled to New York after police roundups following Tsar Alexander II's assassination.

citation.quote: They had fled the police roundups that followed Tsar Alexander II's assassination in 1882 and now found themselves condemned to live as part of the masses that they preferred to fetishize from afar.

title: Birth of Sam Rothbort
summary: The author's great-grandfather Samuel Rothbort was born in Volkovysk, in the Grodno Governorate of the Pale of Settlement, a year after Tsar Alexander II's murder.

citation.quote: My great-grandfather Samuel Rothbort was born on November 25, 1882, a year after Tsar Alexander II's murder. As luck would have it, the pogrom wave that followed never hit his hometown.

title: Founding of Emancipation of Labor
summary: Pavel Axelrod, Georgi Plekhanov, Leo Deutsch, and Vera Zasulich founded Emancipation of Labor in Geneva, the first Russian Marxist group, which would eventually lead to the creation of the Soviet Union.

citation.quote: In 1883, Axelrod, Plekhanov, their fellow revolutionary Leo Deutsch, and the would-be assassin Vera Zasulich founded Emancipation of Labor, the first Russian Marxist group, which, after four decades of improbable events, would lead to the creation of the Soviet Union.

title: Reb Hersch leaves Volkovysk for America
summary: Sam's father, Reb Hersch, a Talmudic scholar who had transcended his baker father's profession, left Volkovysk for America, where he spent most of Sam's childhood despite detesting the country.

citation.quote: A baker's son who had transcended his father's humble profession to become a Talmudic scholar, Reb Hersch left Volkovysk in 1884 and spent most of Sam's childhood in America, a country he detested for its cheerful impiety and lack of kosher food.

title: Fire destroys much of Volkovysk
summary: A fire destroyed much of Volkovysk when Sam Rothbort was four years old. The town's wooden houses were decimated by fires with such regularity that residents marked the years by them.

citation.quote: Volkovysk's houses were wooden, decimated by fires with such regularity that townsfolk marked the years by how long it had been since a conflagration; a fire destroyed much of the town when Sam was four.

title: New York Jewish garment strike halts industry
summary: A strike by New York Jews brought the entire garment industry to a halt, organized by the Russian Colony years before Pati Kremer's work in Vilna.

citation.quote: In 1886, years before Pati Kremer had started educating her small groups of workers in Vilna, a strike by New York Jews brought the entire garment industry to a halt.

title: Folkstsaytung smuggled into Pale of Settlement
summary: Radicals shipped copies of the socialist Yiddish newspaper Folkstsaytung from New York to the Pale of Settlement, where tsarist censors immediately banned it.

citation.quote: In 1886, radicals shipped copies of the socialist *Folkstsaytung* to the Pale of Settlement, where it was immediately banned by tsarist censors.

title: Pati Srednitskaya returns to Vilna for internal exile
summary: Pati Srednitskaya, a young Jewish revolutionary, returned to her hometown of Vilna at age twenty-three to begin a sentence of internal exile under Okhrana surveillance.

citation.quote: This was the hometown to which a young Jewish woman named Pati Srednitskaya returned in 1890, to begin her sentence of internal exile under the watchful eyes of the Okhrana—the Russian Empire's secret police.

title: Great famine hits Russia
summary: The great famine struck Russia when Sam Rothbort was nine. Cossacks forced peasant families to remain in their villages while the tsar continued grain exports.

citation.quote: Sam was nine years old in 1891, when the great famine hit Russia. His watercolors do not show the skeletal peasant families who were forced to remain in their villages by Cossacks, while the tsar stole their grain so that exports could continue apace.

title: Cholera epidemic kills Chaya Ruchl Rothbort
summary: Cholera struck the Russian Empire in 1892, killing half a million people including Sam Rothbort's mother Chaya Ruchl. She was buried in the section of Volkovysk's Jewish cemetery reserved for cholera victims.

citation.quote: Next year came cholera. By the end of 1892, five hundred thousand residents of the Russian Empire were dead. Sam's mother, Chaya Ruchl, was one of them.

title: Arkady Kremer begins writing On Agitation
summary: As the Vilna Group's worker organizing flourished across the Pale, Arkady Kremer decided to write up the conclusions he drew from its success in a pamphlet that became On Agitation.

citation.quote: In 1893, as the movement flourished, Arkady decided to write up the conclusions he drew from its success.

title: On Agitation spreads from Vilna
summary: In the spring of 1894, Arkady Kremer's pamphlet On Agitation began to circulate, reaching Moscow where it was hectographed and distributed to radicals across the Russian Empire.

citation.quote: In the spring of 1894, *On Agitation* began to move. A copy reached Moscow, where it was immediately hectographed and distributed to radicals around the empire.

title: Julius Martov's May Day speech in Vilna
summary: Julius Martov, a young Jewish writer exiled to Vilna, delivered a May Day speech arguing Jewish workers must organize as both workers and Jews, an idea that became the Vilna Group's lodestar.

citation.quote: That's why an 1894 May Day speech by the Vilna Group's Julius Martov had such a bracing effect.

title: Martov returns to Saint Petersburg and forms Union of Struggle
summary: Police allowed Julius Martov to return to Saint Petersburg, where he gathered comrades including Vladimir Ilych Ulyanov to form the Union of Struggle for the Emancipation of the Working Class—the first Marxist group inside Russia proper.

citation.quote: In 1895, police had allowed Julius Martov, the young writer whose May Day speech did so much to chart the Vilna Group's course, to return to his close-knit family in Saint Petersburg.

title: Martov delivers 'The Turning Point' speech
summary: Julius Martov's 1895 speech 'The Turning Point' first clearly articulated the Bund's intersectional approach to Jewish identity politics within the socialist movement.

citation.quote: His 1895 speech “The Turning Point” first clearly articulated their intersectional approach. Eight years later, Martov had rejected its content.

title: Puerto Rican flag first flown in New York
summary: The Puerto Rican flag was first raised at Chimney Corner Hall at Broadway and Wall Street, during a meeting of the Revolutionary Committee of Puerto Rico.

citation.quote: The Puerto Rican flag first flew in 1895, not in San Juan but at Chimney Corner Hall, on the intersection of Broadway and Wall Street, at a meeting of the Revolutionary Committee of Puerto Rico.

title: Okhrana arrests Union of Struggle leaders
summary: The Okhrana arrested the entire Saint Petersburg Union of Struggle for the Emancipation of the Working Class and exiled its leaders Ulyanov and Martov to Siberia.

citation.quote: In December, they arrested the entire group and exiled Ulyanov and Martov to Siberia.

title: Emancipation of Labor group prints On Agitation
summary: The Geneva-based Emancipation of Labor group—Plekhanov, Axelrod, Deutsch, and Zasulich, the four founders of Russian Marxism—printed their own edition of Kremer's On Agitation.

citation.quote: ...it was read by Georgi Plekhanov, Pavel Axelrod, Leo Deutsch, and Vera Zasulich, the four founders of Russian Marxism, who had spent the last decade in fractious exile. They printed their own edition in 1896.

title: Plekhanov speaks at Second International's Fourth Congress
summary: Georgi Plekhanov led the first delegation of exiled Russian socialists to the Second International's fourth congress in London, praising the Vilna Group and calling for a unified Russian social democratic party.

citation.quote: That summer, Georgi Plekhanov led a delegation of exiled Russian socialists to the fourth congress of the Second International, held in London—the main gathering for socialist parties from around the world.

title: Founding of the Bund in Vilna
summary: The Bund, a sometimes-clandestine socialist, secular, and defiantly Jewish political party, was founded in the city of Vilna in the Russian Empire.

citation.quote: Founded in 1897 in the city of Vilna in the Russian Empire, and reaching its height in interwar Poland, the Bund was a sometimes-clandestine political party whose tenets were humane, socialist, secular, and defiantly Jewish.

title: Medem enters University of Kyiv as Bund is founded
summary: Medem entered medical school at the University of Kyiv in 1897, the same year the Bund was founded. By that time he had lost both parents and his Christian faith.

citation.quote: Medem entered medical school at the University of Kyiv in 1897, the year the Bund was born.

title: Political Zionism makes its global debut
summary: Political Zionism made its global debut in 1897, the same year as the Bund, when the inaugural Zionist congress filled a Swiss casino and turned Theodor Herzl into a superstar.

citation.quote: Political Zionism had made its global debut in 1897, the same year as the Bund, and the two groups had been enemies from the start.

title: Antonio Mattei Lluberas leads Yabucoa uprising
summary: Antonio Mattei Lluberas purchased thirty thousand machetes and, with the assistance of the Revolutionary Committee of Puerto Rico, set out to lead an uprising in Yabucoa.

citation.quote: Two years later, with the committee's assistance, Antonio Mattei Lluberas would purchase thirty thousand machetes and, waving that new flag, set out to lead an uprising in Yabucoa.

title: Abe Cahan launches The Forward
summary: In the year the Bund was born, Abe Cahan launched The Forward in New York City, which would become America's most popular Yiddish newspaper.

citation.quote: In 1897, the year the Bund was born, Abe Cahan launched *The Forward* in New York City.

title: Roman Dmowski co-founds the National Democrats
summary: Co-founded by right-wing pamphleteer Roman Dmowski in 1897, the National Democrats (Endeks) built Polish nationalism on antipathy toward Jews.

citation.quote: Co-founded by right-wing pamphleteer Roman Dmowski in 1897, the National Democrats, or Endeks, had spent the last twenty years building their Polish nationalism not upon the armed struggle for independence but upon genocidal antipathy toward the country's Jews.

title: Theodor Herzl founds the Zionist Congress in Basel
summary: Theodor Herzl set up the Zionist Congress in a Basel casino; it would later become the body to which the Jewish Agency answered.

citation.quote: The Jewish Agency answered to the Zionist Congress, that same body that Theodor Herzl set up in a Basel casino in 1897.

title: Police arrest Pati Kremer
summary: Just before the Bund's founding conference, police in Vilna arrested Pati Kremer, leaving Arkady to convene the gathering without her.

citation.quote: Then, in late September the police arrested Pati Kremer.

title: Founding conference of the Bund
summary: Arkady Kremer convened the Bund's founding conference on the evening of Yom Kippur in a safe-house attic in the Vilna suburb of Lukiskes, with thirteen comrades—five intellectuals and eight workers—pledging to fight for both general Russian political demands and the specific interests of Jewish workers.

citation.quote: Arkady set the Bund's founding conference for October 5, 1897, on the evening of Yom Kippur.

title: Police seize Bund presses and arrest Arkady Kremer
summary: Three months after the RSDLP congress, police seized the Bund's printing presses in Minsk and Bobruysk, arrested at least forty-five members, and took Arkady Kremer from his parents' home—his mother collapsed in a stroke as he was led away.

citation.quote: Three months later, police seized the Bund's printing presses in Minsk and Bobruysk and grabbed at least forty-five members. They found Arkady at his parents' home.

title: Bund dispatches Chaim Nemzer to Volkovysk
summary: The Bund sent Chaim Nemzer, a young tutor, from Vilna to Volkovysk in the summer of 1898, where he found fertile ground to organize workers including Sam Rothbort.

citation.quote: The party's name spread from gangsters to factory workers to itinerant agitators, like a young tutor named Chaim Nemzer, whom the Bund dispatched from Vilna to Volkovysk in the summer of 1898.

title: Bund foreign committee launched in Geneva
summary: Launched in 1898 in Geneva, the Bund's foreign committee attracted Exileland's idealistic Jewish students, spreading Bund ideology to European capitals and beyond.

citation.quote: Launched in 1898 in Geneva, the foreign committee quickly attracted a following amongst Exileland's idealistic, footloose Jewish students.

title: Bund co-founds the RSDLP
summary: When the Bund co-founded the Russian Social Democratic Labor Party in 1898, they were the largest, best-organized socialist group in the Russian Empire, entering as an autonomous entity representing the Yiddish working class.

citation.quote: When the Bund co-founded the RSDLP in 1898, they were the largest, best-organized socialist group in the Russian Empire. The Bund entered the new party as an autonomous entity whose turf was the Yiddish working class.

title: First congress of the Russian Social Democratic Labor Party
summary: The RSDLP held its first congress in Minsk; the Bund found the safe house, ran security, sent three of the nine attendees, and joined the party as an independent organization for the Jewish proletariat.

citation.quote: Next March, the Russian Social Democratic Labor Party held its first congress in Minsk. The Bund found the safe house, ran the security, and sent three out of the nine attendees.

title: Okhrana mass arrests of Marxists across the empire
summary: Days after the RSDLP's first congress, the Okhrana arrested five hundred members of various Marxist groups around the Russian Empire to quash the new party.

citation.quote: Though the RSDLP was tiny, the Okhrana moved fast to quash it. Days after the congress, police arrested five hundred members of various Marxist grouplets around the empire.

title: Volkovysk apprentices' Yom Kippur strike
summary: After Rosh Hashanah, Volkovysk Bundists organized apprentices to strike for Saturday nights off; following the Days of Awe and Yom Kippur, bosses conceded and Sam Rothbort never worked another Saturday night in Volkovysk.

citation.quote: Apprentices loathed those Saturday nights, and that September of 1898, Volkovysk Bundists decided to take advantage of their hate. Just after Rosh Hashanah, whispers began in the workshops.

title: Cossacks break up Saint Petersburg student party
summary: Cossack troops broke up a student street party in Saint Petersburg, beating and arresting students. Thirty thousand students went on strike in solidarity, including those at the University of Kyiv.

citation.quote: In February 1899, Cossack troops broke up a student street party in Saint Petersburg.

title: Medem arrested and exiled from Kyiv
summary: After three months on the strike's central committee writing communiqués, Medem and his classmates were arrested by Cossacks. He was exiled back to Minsk and banned from university for life.

citation.quote: He spent three feverish months dashing off communiqués demanding amnesty for the Saint Petersburg students and his striking classmates until, one June morning, Cossacks arrested them all. A few days later, Medem was exiled back to Minsk and banned from university for life.

title: New York City Race Riot
summary: For five days, Irish mobs attacked Black neighborhoods in New York after a Black man named Arthur Harris defended his wife from an undercover cop.

citation.quote: 1900 was the year of the so-called New York City Race Riot, when, for five days, Irish mobs attacked Black neighborhoods, furious because a Black man named Arthur Harris had defended his wife from an undercover cop.

title: Medem publishes first article in Bundist newspaper
summary: On May Day 1900, a Bundist newspaper published Medem's first article after his initial attempts at organizing Christian railway workers had failed.

citation.quote: Medem had more success as a writer, and on May Day 1900, a Bundist newspaper published his first article.

title: Kautsky writes on the Jewish proletariat
summary: The Marxist theoretician Karl Kautsky published his characterization of Russian Jewish workers as 'the pariah among pariahs,' trapped in a spiral of unemployment and poverty under racist legal restrictions.

citation.quote: "The Russian Jewish proletariat is the pariah among pariahs," wrote the Marxist theoretician Karl Kautsky in 1901.

title: Medem arrested in Minsk roundup
summary: Police rounded up Minsk organizers in 1901, with Medem among them. On the prison intake form he wrote his nationality as 'Jew' without hesitation.

citation.quote: In 1901, police rounded up a passel of Minsk organizers, Medem among them. At the prison, he wrote down his nationality on the intake form. Jew.

title: Medem arrives in Exileland
summary: After skipping bail following his Minsk arrest, Medem navigated a purgatory of safe houses to escape the Russian Empire, arriving in Berne in 1901.

citation.quote: Medem arrived in Exileland in 1901. After his arrest in Minsk, he'd skipped bail and navigated a purgatory of safe houses to escape the Russian Empire, making his way to Berne.

title: Foreign committee reunites Pati with Arkady Kremer in London
summary: In 1902, after Arkady Kremer fled to London following two years' imprisonment in Moscow, the Bund's foreign committee arranged for Pati to join him there.

citation.quote: When, after two years' imprisonment in Moscow, Arkady Kremer fled Russia, the foreign committee eased his way to London. In 1902, they arranged for Pati to join him.

title: Bund becomes largest revolutionary party in Russia
summary: By 1902, the Bund was the largest revolutionary party in Russia, with thirty thousand members, and Volkovysk hosted an energetic cell that robbed liquor stores and freed political prisoners.

citation.quote: By 1902, the Bund was the largest revolutionary party in Russia, with thirty thousand members, and Volkovysk hosted an energetic little cell.

title: Lenin publishes What Is to Be Done
summary: In his 1902 pamphlet, Lenin argued that only a ruthlessly centralized party of obedient professional revolutionaries could seize power in Russia.

citation.quote: In his 1902 pamphlet *What Is to Be Done,* Lenin spelled out his belief that only a ruthlessly centralized party of obedient professional revolutionaries had a chance of seizing power in Russia.

title: Lenin maneuvers to exclude Bund from RSDLP committee
summary: After police arrested half of the RSDLP's organizing committee in early 1902, Lenin stacked the new committee with his partisans by ensuring the Bund's invitations were never sent.

citation.quote: Lenin had long yearned to subordinate the Bund, and he saw his chance in early 1902. After police arrested half of the RSDLP’s organizing committee, Lenin decided to shape the new committee to his liking. Mysteriously, the Bund’s invitations were never sent.

title: May Day march defies Governor von Wahl in Vilna
summary: After Governor Victor von Wahl forbade any May Day celebrations in Vilna in 1902, Polish and Jewish workers marched anyway. Cossacks charged with whips, making thirty arrests; the detainees were later stripped and beaten.

citation.quote: Lekert made his name in 1902, in Vilna, after Governor Victor von Wahl forbade any May Day celebrations. Polish and Jewish workers marched anyway. Cossacks charged them with whips. Thirty arrests.

title: Hirsh Lekert attempts to assassinate Governor von Wahl
summary: On the night of May 18, Hirsh Lekert fired twice at Governor von Wahl as he left the Lushinka circus, but the bullets only grazed von Wahl's leg. Lekert was hanged a few weeks later.

citation.quote: On the night of May 18, von Wahl and his cronies stumbled out of the Lushinka circus. Hirsh Lekert fired twice, but the bullets only grazed von Wahl's leg. Thanks to the intervention of the minister of the interior, Vyacheslav von Plehve, a military court hanged Lekert a few weeks later.

title: Medem speaks at Bund's fifth conference in Zurich
summary: Medem's ideas got their first major public hearing at the Bund's fifth conference in Zurich in 1903. Debate over his views on nationality grew so violent the matter was struck from the official record.

citation.quote: Medem's ideas got their first major public hearing in 1903 in Zurich, at the Bund's fifth conference.

title: Bund withdraws from the RSDLP
summary: After six weeks of argument continued in London, Martov demanded the Bund delete a rule giving it the right to organize Jewish workers wherever it liked. The Bund lost the vote 41 to 5, and Liber announced the Bund's withdrawal from the RSDLP.

citation.quote: The congress had dragged on for six weeks when Martov put the Bund out of its misery. He demanded the Bund delete a paragraph of its rules that gave it the right to organize Jewish workers wherever it liked. It was a referendum on the party’s autonomy. When the vote came, the Bund lost, 41–5.

title: Bolshevik–Menshevik split
summary: With the Bund gone, Lenin had just enough delegates to win the vote on party membership, labeling Martov's faction 'Mensheviks' (Minorityites) and his own side 'Bolsheviks' (Majorityites).

citation.quote: With the Bund gone, Lenin had just enough delegates to win. Ever astute on matters of branding, Lenin labeled Martov’s crew “Minorityites,” or *Mensheviks.* He seized the term “Majorityite” for his side. In Russian, the word is *Bolshevik.*

title: Sixth Zionist Congress in Basel
summary: On his way home from the RSDLP congress, Medem stopped in Basel to observe the sixth world congress of the Zionists, where Theodor Herzl spoke of his meeting with Russian interior minister von Plehve.

citation.quote: On the way home from one interminable political gathering full of enemies, Medem stopped by Basel, Switzerland, to observe another group of antagonists—the Zionists, who were in the midst of their sixth world congress.

title: Weizmann names the Bund as Zionism's hardest struggle
summary: Chaim Weizmann, the Zionist leader who later became the first president of Israel, wrote in 1903 that 'our hardest struggle everywhere is conducted against [the Jewish Labor Bund].'

citation.quote: Chaim Weizmann, the Zionist leader who later became the first president of Israel, wrote in 1903 that “our hardest struggle everywhere is conducted against \[the Jewish Labor Bund\],” while the Bund described Zionism as “the most evil enemy of the organized Jewish proletariat.”

title: Volkovysk pogrom and self-defense killing of two policemen
summary: At the end of 1903, a pogrom in Volkovysk was met by a Bund self-defense militia under Naum L'vovich; his unit opened fire on two policemen leading a plundering crowd, killing both on the spot.

citation.quote: In his application, L’vovich described a pogrom in Volkovysk that took place at the end of 1903. L’vovich wrote that he had commanded a unit of ten fighters in the defense of one of Volkovysk’s main squares. Two policemen led a crowd hunting for Jewish stalls to plunder.

title: Liuba Levinson drowns in Orchard Street bathtub
summary: During the 1903 heat wave, Bundist pioneer Liuba Levinson grew dizzy in a bath and drowned at age thirty-seven, having intended to leave her baby with her sister and return to Russia.

citation.quote: During the heat wave of 1903, Liuba drew herself a bath. Once in the tub, she grew dizzy. Her head slipped below the water. Liuba Levinson was thirty-seven years old when she drowned in that kitchen bathtub.

title: Trotsky breaks with Lenin at the second RSDLP congress
summary: Trotsky broke with Lenin during the tumultuous second RSDLP congress of 1903, eventually splitting from Martov's Mensheviks as well to become a party of one.

citation.quote: Trotsky had broken with Lenin during the tumultuous second RSDLP congress of 1903, but he soon split as well from Julius Martov's Mensheviks, who dominated the Saint Petersburg Soviet, the revolution's organizing body in the capital.

title: Gina Bizenzwieg first hears Medem speak
summary: During a visit to Switzerland in 1903, the teenage Gina Bizenzwieg first heard Vladimir Medem speak but couldn't get close because groupies surrounded him.

citation.quote: She first heard Medem speak during a visit to Switzerland in 1903, but groupies surrounded him, and she couldn't get close.

title: Kishinev pogrom
summary: Over three days in April 1903, Christians in Kishinev raped dozens of Jewish women and murdered forty-five Jews, drawing international press coverage that made the town's name synonymous with anti-Jewish massacre.

citation.quote: Whipped up by a local newspaper editor, over the course of three days in April 1903, Kishinev Christians raped dozens of Jewish women and murdered forty-five Jews.

title: RSDLP Second Congress begins in Brussels
summary: The Russian Social Democratic Labor Party's second congress began in Brussels on July 17, 1903, with delegates meeting in a flea-infested wool worker's cooperative; Iskra had stacked the agenda and only five of fifty-one delegates were Bundists.

citation.quote: When the Russian Social Democratic Labor Party’s second congress began in Brussels on July 17, 1903, few realized it would have cataclysmic effects on the Bund’s future.

title: Bund self-defense beats back pogrom in Gomel
summary: In September 1903, two hundred Bund self-defense youth beat back a pogrom in Gomel carried out by Christian railway workers; the pogromists only managed to kill seven Jews.

citation.quote: In September 1903, two hundred of these youth beat back a pogrom in Gomel, a mostly Jewish town not far from Kishinev, which was carried out by Christian railway workers who were supposed to be their proletarian brothers. The pogromists only managed to kill seven Jews.

title: Volkovysk Revolutionary Union founded
summary: A small group of Bundist immigrants gathered in a tenement on 56 Orchard Street and founded the Volkovysk Revolutionary Union, printing membership cards and electing a board.

citation.quote: On November 11, 1903, a small group of Bundist immigrants gathered in a tenement on 56 Orchard Street and founded the Volkovysk Revolutionary Union.

title: Arkady Kremer arrives in New York
summary: Arkady Kremer arrived from London to be greeted by a rally organized by labor lawyer Meyer London, while Pati Kremer made the arrangements.

citation.quote: In December 1903, Arkady Kremer arrived from London. Pati was already in town making arrangements.

title: Sam Rothbort arrives in America
summary: Sam Rothbort, the author's great-grandfather, emigrated from Volkovysk to the New World, beginning the family line in America.

citation.quote: These photos, as much as his paintings, fleshed out his image as Artist Progenitor, who brought the family line to the New World in 1904 and remained alive long enough to see my parents wed.

title: Bund declares pogroms exist where the government wants them
summary: In 1904, the Bund had written that 'pogroms exist only where the government wants them,' a claim borne out by the events of 1905.

citation.quote: In 1904, the Bund had written that "pogroms exist only where the government wants them," and the events of 1905 proved them right.

title: Sam Rothbort joins Volkovysk Revolutionary Union in New York
summary: Sam Rothbort joined the Volkovysk Revolutionary Union (later Workmen's Circle branch 100) as a young exile in New York in 1904.

citation.quote: I found the program for the fiftieth-anniversary banquet of Workmen's Circle branch 100—formerly the Volkovysk Revolutionary Union, which Sam had joined in 1904 as a young exile in New York.

title: Sam Rothbort boards ship from Antwerp
summary: After fleeing Volkovysk following the pogrom and the killing of Officer Chugunchik, Sam Rothbort made his way through Germany to the port of Antwerp, where on March 19 he boarded his ship to America.

citation.quote: From there he rode the rails 625 miles to the port city of Antwerp. On March 19, he boarded his ship.

title: Sam Rothbort arrives in New York
summary: Sam Rothbort's ship docked in New York City, beginning his life as a Jewish immigrant on the Lower East Side.

citation.quote: Sam's ship docked on March 30, 1904.

title: Orchard Street asphalt workers strike
summary: A hundred asphalt workers threw rocks at scabs on Orchard Street during a strike.

citation.quote: In April 1904, on Orchard Street, a hundred asphalt workers threw rocks at scabs.

title: Fifty thousand garment workers strike
summary: Fifty thousand garment workers struck in New York, with seamstresses arguing with male strikers in coffee shops on Ludlow, Suffolk, and Forsyth streets.

citation.quote: In July, fifty thousand garment workers struck, with *The New York Times* remarking that the seamstresses "get into all sorts of arguments with the men strikers when they meet in the little coffee shops of Ludlow, Suffolk and Forsyth."

title: Assassination of Vyacheslav von Plehve
summary: A terrorist from the Socialist Revolutionary Party killed Russian minister of the interior Vyacheslav von Plehve, sparking celebrations on the Lower East Side and a Forward party hosted by Abe Cahan.

citation.quote: In July 1904, they would have joined the spontaneous celebrations that broke out when a terrorist belonging to the peasant-populist Socialist Revolutionary Party killed that arch-antisemite, the minister of the interior Vyacheslav von Plehve.

title: Structural Building Trades Alliance strike
summary: Forty thousand members of the Structural Building Trades Alliance unions walked off the job; Sam Rothbort could not join because the painters' union banned Jews.

citation.quote: Then, in August, forty thousand members of the Structural Building Trades Alliance unions walked off the job.

title: Viktor Alter joins the Bund
summary: At age fifteen, Viktor Alter joined the Bund during the 1905 revolution. His leadership of a student strike earned him a lifetime ban from Russian universities.

citation.quote: Alter had joined the Bund during the 1905 revolution at age fifteen. His leadership of a student strike earned him a lifetime ban from Russian universities.

title: Bund self-defense militias impress Jabotinsky
summary: During the revolution of 1905, the Bund's self-defense militias impressed Vladimir Jabotinsky, leading him to view Bundists as his greatest rivals.

citation.quote: During the revolution of 1905, the Bund's self-defense militias impressed Jabotinsky, leading him to view Bundists as his greatest rivals.

title: Abramovich publishes To Arms pamphlet
summary: Days after the Bloody Sunday massacre, Bundist orator Raphael Abramovich in Dvinsk wrote the pamphlet To Arms, urging armed revolution.

citation.quote: Now a prominent Bundist orator, days after the massacre, he dashed off a pamphlet called To Arms:

title: Bloody Sunday massacre at the Winter Palace
summary: Father Gapon led 50,000 workers in a peaceful march to the Winter Palace in Saint Petersburg; soldiers opened fire, killing at least 130 people and igniting the 1905 revolution.

citation.quote: Marxist schematics said that Russia was not ripe for revolution, Medem thought, and he had never heard of Father Gapon, the former priest who, the night before, on January 22, 1905, had led fifty thousand workers on a march toward the Winter Palace, home of Tsar Nicholas II.

title: Bloody Sunday reported in The Forward
summary: Sam Rothbort read The Forward's front page reporting the St. Petersburg massacre later known as Bloody Sunday, with thousands of strikers murdered and revolution breaking out.

citation.quote: Then, on the morning of January 23, 1905, Sam looked at the front page of *The Forward,* and his old home, with all its idealism and carnage, came crashing back.

title: Saint Petersburg general strike after Bloody Sunday
summary: The morning after Bloody Sunday, 160,000 Saint Petersburg workers walked out on strike in response to the massacre.

citation.quote: The next morning 160,000 Saint Petersburg workers walked out on strike.

title: Riga conference unites socialist parties
summary: The Bund persuaded rival socialist parties from across the Russian empire to meet in Riga, agreeing on a list of liberal demands including a constituent assembly.

citation.quote: With great difficulty, the Bund persuaded this alphabet soup of groups to hold a conference in Riga in February, where they agreed on a list of liberal demands including the right to vote, freedom for political prisoners, an eight-hour workday, free speech, a free press, the separation of church and state, and, the most cherished demand of revolutionaries, a freely elected constituent assembly.

title: Krynki uprising
summary: Three weeks after Bloody Sunday, Bundists and socialists in Krynki seized the town for 24 hours before Russian troops retook it, killing 42 workers.

citation.quote: Three weeks after Bloody Sunday, Bundists and socialists in the Polish town of Krynki called a mass meeting in a synagogue to incite a general strike. With the 1,500 people who showed up, they proceeded to take over the city.

title: Bund central committee meets secretly in Dvinsk
summary: Twenty Bundists gathered at a covert headquarters in Dvinsk to plan strategy, including arms smuggling from Belgium and propaganda directed at conscripted soldiers.

citation.quote: On February 15, on the other side of the world, twenty Bundists gathered in Dvinsk, where the central committee had set up its secret headquarters inside a covertly rented apartment.

title: Dvinsk general strike and killing of Aba Reich
summary: Around early March, the Bund called a general strike in Dvinsk that escalated into days of street fighting; a teenage worker named Aba Reich was shot and given a mass funeral.

citation.quote: Arkady Kremer missed the Bund's conference in Dvinsk, but he was likely there two weeks later when the party proclaimed a general strike, one of hundreds they would call in the coming months.

title: Bundist battle squads begin assassinating police
summary: By the end of March 1905, a growing number of police officials were gunned down by Bundist battle squads or killed with homemade 'matzoh ball' bombs in retaliation for state violence.

citation.quote: By the end of March, a growing number of police officials would be gunned down by Bundist battle squads, or dispatched by clever little explosives, nicknamed "matzoh balls," hurled by guys who turned up later in Brooklyn under unassuming American names.

title: Strike at Grohman's textile factory in Lodz
summary: Strikes broke out at Grohman's textile factory in Lodz; Cossacks shot three workers, and fifty thousand people attended their funeral, setting off a cycle of unrest.

citation.quote: The Russo-Japanese war was wrecking the Lodz economy, and after strikes broke out at Grohman's textile factory on May 16, 1905, Cossacks shot three workers. Fifty thousand people attended their funeral.

title: Police kill Little Bund children in Lodz
summary: Police attacked a weekly parade of the Little Bund on Wschodnia Street, shooting two boys and kicking a third to death, escalating the Lodz conflict.

citation.quote: On May 27, the conflict escalated when the police turned their attention to Wschodnia Street and to the Little Bund, which was enjoying their weekly parade.

title: Lodz strike reaches 35,000 workers
summary: By May 30, thirty-five thousand people were out on strike in Lodz, with workers ruling the streets at night after police retreated.

citation.quote: By May 30, thirty-five thousand people were out on strike. Crowds wandered the city, red flags in hand, until police dispersed them.

title: Lodz uprising and barricades
summary: Following the burials of victims, fifty thousand workers marched in Lodz; Cossacks fired into the crowd killing eighteen, and the next morning workers built barricades under twenty-two-year-old Virgil Kahan, igniting a multiethnic insurrection.

citation.quote: The next morning, workers began building barricades on the Bundist birzhes on Wschodnia and Poludniowe streets, under the leadership of the twenty-two-year-old Virgil Kahan.

title: Cossacks fire on Odesa strikers at Henn's factory
summary: After informants tipped off police about a planned general strike in Odesa's Peresyp district, Cossacks fired into a crowd of protesters at Henn's factory, triggering a citywide walkout.

citation.quote: On June 13, protesters gathered at Henn's factory. Cossacks fired into the crowd. When the news spread, workers across Odesa walked off their jobs.

title: Battleship Potemkin anchors in Odesa harbor
summary: The mutinied battleship Potemkin arrived in Odesa flying a red flag, after sailors led by Vakulenchuk overthrew their officers in a protest over rations.

citation.quote: On June 15, in the opal hour before sunrise, Anna Lipshitz heard the news, alongside the rest of the city. A battleship named Potemkin had just dropped anchor in Odesa's port. It was flying a red flag.

title: Lodz picnic massacre on Lagiewnicka Street
summary: After a joint Bund and Polish socialist picnic outside Lodz, marchers returning to town clashed with an army detachment on Lagiewnicka Street; five Jewish and Polish protesters were killed.

citation.quote: On June 18, the Bund and Lodz's two Polish socialist parties hosted a joint picnic in the nearby forest. Thousands of Jewish and Polish workers came... On Lagiewnicka Street, they ran into an army detachment. Someone shot a pistol—each side blamed the other—and by the time the chaos stopped, five Polish and Jewish protesters were dead.

title: Martial law declared in Lodz
summary: Lodz came under martial law on June 26; authorities killed 561 people, most of them Jews, over eight days to put down the rebellion.

citation.quote: On June 26, Lodz came under martial law. The prisons overflowed with Jewish socialists. Over eight days, authorities killed 561 people to put down the rebellion.

title: Medem awaits Abramovich in Zurich for Bund congress
summary: At the start of October, Medem and the Bund's foreign committee gathered in Zurich, having smuggled their leaders over the border to prepare for the sixth party congress.

citation.quote: At the beginning of October, Medem awaited Abramovich's arrival in Zurich. For months, he and the rest of the Bund's foreign committee had been preparing for the sixth party congress—a momentous occasion in these revolutionary times—and at last they had succeeded in smuggling most of their leaders over the border.

title: Pogroms erupt across the Russian Empire after the manifesto
summary: Within hours of the October Manifesto's publication, police opened fire on protesters across the empire, and over twelve days pogroms broke out in 690 towns and cities.

citation.quote: Within hours of the manifesto's publication, street celebrations turned to horror as police opened fire on protesters in cities around the empire.

title: Tsar Nicholas II issues the October Manifesto
summary: After four days of general strike, Tsar Nicholas II published the October Manifesto, legalizing political parties, easing newspaper publication, and establishing a duma with limited powers.

citation.quote: The revolution had forced the absolute autocrat to acknowledge his people. The palace published the manifesto on October 17.

title: Trotsky tears up the manifesto at a Saint Petersburg demonstration
summary: On the day of the October Manifesto, Trotsky addressed hundreds of thousands of protesters in Saint Petersburg, warning them not to trust the tsar and tearing the manifesto to shreds.

citation.quote: On October 17, the day of the Manifesto, Medem was stuck in Exileland, playing the Bund's anthem on the piano of Café Terese. Trotsky was at a Saint Petersburg demonstration, with hundreds of thousands of protesters at his feet.

title: Odesa pogrom begins
summary: The Odesa pogrom began when young Jewish radicals celebrating the October Manifesto in the Moldavanka district clashed with Russian workers, sparking an ethnic riot.

citation.quote: In Odesa, the pogrom began on October 18. Young radicals had gathered in the dusty streets of the city's Jewish Moldavanka district to celebrate the October Manifesto.

title: Odesa pogrom death toll reaches 800
summary: By October 22, pogromists had murdered eight hundred Odesa Jews and left perhaps a hundred thousand more homeless after four days of mob violence.

citation.quote: By October 22, pogromists had murdered eight hundred Odesa Jews, and left perhaps a hundred thousand more homeless.

title: Saint Petersburg Soviet's leader arrested, Trotsky takes over
summary: On November 22, police arrested the Saint Petersburg Soviet's ostensible leader, leaving Trotsky in charge of the revolution's organizing body in the capital.

citation.quote: By November 22, the authorities had had enough. That day, police arrested the soviet's ostensible leader, leaving Trotsky in charge.

title: The New York Age decries persecution of Jews
summary: The Black newspaper The New York Age published a column expressing solidarity with persecuted Jews, writing that they had been persecuted more than any people since the crucifixion.

citation.quote: On November 23: "The Jewish people have been persecuted more than any other people since the crucifixion of Jesus Christ…. Our sympathies are with the persecuted of all races and lands."

title: Medem and Kossovsky cross the Russian border
summary: Disguised in derby hats and fancy suits with fake passports and pistols, Medem and Vladimir Kossovsky arrived at the Russian border on November 27 en route to Dvinsk.

citation.quote: In late November, Medem and his comrade Vladimir Kossovsky stopped by the Bund's office in Geneva to grab fake passports and pistols that they barely knew how to shoot. Disguised in derby hats and fancy suits, they arrived at the Russian border on November 27.

title: The New York Age condemns inaction over Odessa
summary: The New York Age decried the fact that no nation had yet interfered on behalf of Odessa's butchered thousands.

citation.quote: On November 30, they decried the fact that "no nation has yet interfered on behalf of Odessa's butchered thousands."

title: Saint Petersburg Soviet issues financial manifesto
summary: On December 2, the Saint Petersburg Soviet issued a financial manifesto urging everyone to withdraw their money from banks and refuse to pay taxes to starve the tsar of cash.

citation.quote: On December 2, the soviet issued a financial manifesto, urging everyone to withdraw their money from banks and refuse to pay taxes, to starve the tsar of the cash he needed to buy guns.

title: Trotsky arrested at the Saint Petersburg Soviet
summary: Soldiers stormed the Saint Petersburg Soviet's headquarters at the Technological Institute. Trotsky scolded them, declared the session closed, and allowed himself to be arrested with a smile.

citation.quote: The next day, soldiers stormed the soviet's headquarters at the Technological Institute. When they entered the soviet's meeting room, Trotsky coolly scolded them for their interruption. He declared the session closed, as was his prerogative, then allowed himself to be arrested with a smile.

title: 125,000 Jews march in New York to mourn pogrom victims
summary: On Monday, December 4, 1905, 125,000 eastern-European Jews converged on Rutgers Square on the Lower East Side to mourn families murdered in Russian pogroms, led by Joseph Barondess.

citation.quote: On Monday, December 4, 1905, 125,000 eastern-European Jews converged on Rutgers Square, on the Lower East Side, to mourn their families murdered in Russian pogroms.

title: The New York Age compares pogroms to Southern racism
summary: The New York Age wrote that the massacres of Jews in Russia surpassed even the Ku Kluxism, peonage, and chain-gang systems endured by American Black people.

citation.quote: One December 7, they wrote: "The civilized world has never witnessed anything quite so horrible as the massacres of Jews, which are daily taking place in Russia. With the Ku Kluxism, peonage and chain-gang systems in the South, we have believed that the American negro endured the hardest lot of all mankind. We must revise our judgement."

title: American Jewish Yearbook tabulates 47 pogroms after Kishinev
summary: In 1906, the American Jewish Yearbook published a table of forty-seven pogroms that took place in the year after Kishinev, noting that in three cities riots were suppressed by self-defense.

citation.quote: In 1906, the *American Jewish Yearbook* published a table of forty-seven pogroms that took place in the year after Kishinev. In three cities, the table notes, “riots were suppressed by Self Defense.”

title: 125,000 Russian Jews arrive in America
summary: One hundred twenty-five thousand Jews from the Russian Empire arrived in America in 1906, filling the Lower East Side and Williamsburg and overflowing into Brownsville.

citation.quote: One hundred twenty-five thousand Jews from the Russian Empire arrived in America in 1906. They filled the Lower East Side and Williamsburg, then overflowed east, turning Brownsville into a boomtown.

title: Bund membership collapses from 30,000 to 609
summary: After the failed 1905 revolution, the Bund's membership plummeted from thirty thousand in 1906 to just 609 by 1910 as leaders quit, fled, or were arrested.

citation.quote: The Bund had thirty thousand members in 1906. By 1910, this number had plummeted to 609.

title: Vladimir Medem appointed to Bund central committee
summary: In 1906 the Bund appointed Vladimir Medem to its central committee, and he edited a newspaper with Abramovich at the Bund's Vilna office on Chopin Street.

citation.quote: Medem had not imagined things going like this in 1906, when the Bund appointed him to the central committee.

title: S. An-sky publishes novella In Shtrom
summary: S. An-sky's novella In Shtrom is published, featuring a young revolutionary dismissing the Bund as small and pathetic in the face of the empire-wide revolution.

citation.quote: It's all so small, so pathetic and wretched," says a young revolutionary in S. An-sky's 1907 novella *In Shtrom.*

title: Arkady Kremer arrested and tried in Vilna
summary: A decade after founding the Bund, Arkady Kremer was charged in a Vilna court as leader of an illegal political organization. Pati arranged a bribe and affidavit that secured his release after months of pretrial detention.

citation.quote: In 1907, a decade after he had launched the Bund in a safe-house attic, a Vilna court charged Arkady as leader of an illegal political organization.

title: Medem arrives in Berlin, begins years in Exileland
summary: Vladimir Medem arrived in Berlin in 1908 expecting to stay only the summer, but ended up remaining in Western European exile for years alongside hundreds of other Russian radicals.

citation.quote: When Medem arrived in Berlin in 1908, he expected his trip to last the summer. He ended up staying in Exileland for years.

title: Sam Rothbort returns to New York and settles in Williamsburg
summary: After two years working at the Davenport gun factory in Connecticut, Sam Rothbort returned to New York around 1908 and settled in the Jewish neighborhood of South Williamsburg.

citation.quote: After two years of Connecticut exile, he returned to New York around 1908 and planted himself in the East Side's overflow room—the recently Jewish neighborhood of Williamsburg.

title: Yiddish dailies condemn Springfield pogrom
summary: When a white mob attacked Black people in Springfield, Illinois in 1908, New York's Yiddish dailies condemned the 'pogrom' and urged street protests and donations for survivors.

citation.quote: in 1908, when a white mob attacked Black people in Springfield, Illinois, Yiddish dailies didn't merely condemn the "pogrom"; they urged street protests and collected donations for survivors.

title: Frumkin fights for Yiddish at Czernowitz conference
summary: Esther Frumkin famously argued for the supremacy of Yiddish over Hebrew at the first international Yiddish conference in Czernowitz.

citation.quote: She was a single mother with a spartan work ethic, a ferocious intellect, and a jealous fixation on Yiddish, whose supremacy against Hebrew she had famously fought for at the first international Yiddish conference in Czernowitz in 1908.

title: Medem and Gina reunite at Lake Maggiore
summary: In 1909, Gina Bizenzwieg ran into Vladimir Medem at Lake Maggiore in southern Switzerland, where he joined her vacation with student friends. The reunion set her on the path to becoming his caretaker and wife.

citation.quote: She ran into Medem again four years later, in 1909, at Lake Maggiore, in southern Switzerland.

title: Cloak makers' victorious strike
summary: Labor lawyer Meyer London represented fifty thousand cloak makers during their victorious strike of 1910, building the reputation that led to his later congressional bid.

citation.quote: The socialist candidate was Meyer London, now a beloved labor lawyer, who had represented fifty thousand cloak makers during their victorious strike of 1910.

title: Rose Rothbort gives birth to Henry
summary: In 1911 Rose Rothbort gave birth to her first child, a boy named Henry. She then persuaded Sam to leave their Brooklyn apartment for a shared dairy farm in the Catskills.

citation.quote: In 1911, Rose gave birth to their first child, a boy named Henry.

title: Sophia Dubnova and Henryk Erlich marry in Saint Petersburg
summary: Sophia Dubnova and Henryk Erlich married in Saint Petersburg with no family and little fuss; she wore a gray overcoat and resolved to keep her maiden name.

citation.quote: They married in Saint Petersburg the next year, in 1911, with no family and little fuss. She wore a gray overcoat. Henryk messed up the vows. She resolved to keep using her maiden name.

title: Tsarist troops massacre striking workers at Lena goldfields
summary: In 1912 tsarist troops massacred over two hundred striking workers at the Lena goldfields. Public outrage brought a wave of new members to the Bund.

citation.quote: That year, tsarist troops massacred over two hundred striking workers at the Lena goldfields, and the public outrage that followed brought new members to the party.

title: Eugene Debs receives 900,000 votes in presidential election
summary: In the 1912 presidential election, Socialist Party of America candidate Eugene V. Debs received nine hundred thousand votes, an astounding 6 percent of the popular vote.

citation.quote: In the 1912 presidential election, its candidate, Eugene V. Debs, received nine hundred thousand votes, an astounding 6 percent of the popular vote.

title: Viktor Alter returns to Poland
summary: After studying engineering in Belgium and marrying a Belgian socialist, Viktor Alter returned to Poland on party work in 1912. The Okhrana quickly exiled him to Siberia.

citation.quote: He studied engineering in Belgium, married a Belgian socialist, and returned to Poland on party work in 1912. The Okhrana quickly exiled him to Siberia.

title: Medem sent to Vienna to edit Lebens-Fragen
summary: In spring 1912 the Bund sent Vladimir Medem to Vienna to edit a new newspaper called Lebens-Fragen, intended as a legal periodical published out of Warsaw. Warsaw police quickly arrested its entire staff.

citation.quote: In the spring of 1912, the party sent Medem to Vienna to edit a new newspaper called Lebens-Fragen that would be published out of Warsaw.

title: Mendel Beilis tried in Kyiv for ritual murder
summary: In 1913 a Kyiv court tried Jewish factory foreman Mendel Beilis on the charge of ritual murder. The Bund launched protest strikes across the empire, the jury acquitted Beilis, and the trial won thousands of new recruits for the Bund.

citation.quote: The next year, in 1913, a Kyiv court tried a Jewish factory foreman named Mendel Beilis on the sensational charge of ritual murder.

title: Medem and Gina return to the Russian Empire
summary: Ignoring Abramovich's warning, Medem and Gina boarded a train toward the Russian Empire at the end of 1913 after Gina threatened suicide over their isolation in Vienna.

citation.quote: He and Gina boarded a train toward the Russian Empire at the end of 1913.

title: Rothborts return to Brooklyn from Catskills farm
summary: After their Catskills dairy farming experiment with three other families collapsed, the Rothborts returned to Brooklyn in 1913, with Rose possibly pregnant with daughter Ida.

citation.quote: The Rothborts returned to Brooklyn in 1913. Rose may have been pregnant again, this time with my great-aunt Ida.

title: Amalgamated and ILGWU represent over 100,000 workers
summary: By 1914, former Bundists Sidney Hillman's Amalgamated Clothing Workers and David Dubinsky's International Ladies Garment Workers Union together represented over a hundred thousand workers and had wrung concessions through massive strikes.

citation.quote: By 1914, their two groups represented over a hundred thousand workers between them and had wrung concessions from employers through massive strikes.

title: Meyer London wins congressional election
summary: In the 1914 congressional elections, socialist Meyer London defeated Tammany Hall's Henry Goldfogle. Fifty thousand people gathered in front of the Forward Building on election night to celebrate the victory.

citation.quote: By the time the 1914 congressional elections rolled around, excitement among New York's Jewish neighborhoods was at a boil.

title: Outbreak of the Great War
summary: After Princip's assassination of Franz Ferdinand, Austria-Hungary attacked Serbia with Germany's help. Bulgaria and the Ottoman Empire joined the Central Powers; mutual defense pacts drew England, France, and tsarist Russia in as the Allies.

citation.quote: The Great War began with all the inevitability of a Grecian play. After Princip assassinated Franz Ferdinand, Austria-Hungary attacked Serbia, with the help of its ally Germany. Bristling from defeats in the Balkan Wars, Bulgaria and the Ottoman Empire soon joined up on Austria's side.

title: Collapse of the Second International
summary: The Second International collapsed as the Social Democratic Party of Germany voted to fund its country's war effort; socialist parties in other belligerent countries followed, abandoning international brotherhood for nationalism.

citation.quote: The Second International, the worldwide organization of socialist parties, of which the Bund was a member, was supposed to prevent wars like this. Yet it collapsed like a meringue on a humid day. First, the Social Democratic Party of Germany, the biggest, most powerful socialist party in Europe, betrayed Marx's adage that the working man had no country and voted to fund their country's war.

title: Assassination of Jean Jaurès
summary: French socialist leader Jean Jaurès, who sought to avert France's entry into the war, was shot in the back by a nationalist while dining at Montmartre's Café du Croissant; a Parisian jury declared the murderer innocent.

citation.quote: The famed socialist leader Jean Jaurès had sought to avert France's entry into the conflict. He was dining at Montmartre's Café du Croissant when a nationalist shot him in the back; a Parisian jury declared his murderer innocent of any crime.

title: Bund statement on the war
summary: The Bund issued a statement calling for international socialists to put pressure on warring governments for a peace without annexations or indemnities: "Down with the war. Long live international brotherhood."

citation.quote: The Bund's 1914 statement is typical of this view. "International socialists must strive to put an end to this bloodbath" by putting pressure on the warring governments to make a peace without annexations or indemnities. "Down with the war. Long live international brotherhood."

title: Russian wartime ban on the Yiddish press and Jewish conscription
summary: Overnight, the Russian government banned the Yiddish press. The military drafted four hundred thousand Jews, including many of the Bund's best activists, while police arrested leaders like Mark Liber.

citation.quote: Overnight, the government banned the Yiddish press. The military drafted four hundred thousand Jews, including many of the Bund's best activists, while police rounded up leaders like Mark Liber in the wave of arrests that accompanied mobilization.

title: Mass deportation of Jews from the Pale of Settlement
summary: The Russian empire's top general ordered mass deportations of Jews east into central Russia, fearing they would assist advancing enemy armies. Within months, over 200,000 people were made homeless, often with as little as twelve hours to pack.

citation.quote: The Pale of Settlement was now a front line, and the military viewed its five million Jewish inhabitants as potential spies. Fearing Jews would assist the advancing enemy armies, the empire's top general ordered mass deportations east, to central Russia. Within months, over two hundred thousand people were made homeless.

title: Russian army invades Galicia and Bukovina
summary: Through the autumn of 1914, the Russian army advanced into the Austro-Hungarian provinces of Galicia and Bukovina, where 900,000 Jews had enjoyed quasi-equality under Habsburg rule. Pogroms followed, with Jews fired from government jobs and businesses sacked.

citation.quote: Through the autumn of 1914, the Russian army advanced into the Austro-Hungarian Empire. They marched into the provinces of Galicia and Bukovina, where nine hundred thousand Jews had enjoyed quasi-equality for the past two centuries under liberal Habsburg rule. This ended overnight.

title: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo
summary: Gavrilo Princip, a teenage assassin for Serbia's Black Hand Society, killed Austria's Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo, triggering the chain of alliances that led to World War I.

citation.quote: So it went. Tap tap tap. Seconds. Minutes. Hours. Days. Until one balmy afternoon in June, when Gina told him that Austria's archduke, Franz Ferdinand, had taken a wrong turn in Sarajevo, into an unplanned encounter with Gavrilo Princip, teenage assassin for Serbia's ultranationalist Black Hand Society.

title: German army pushes Russia out of Galicia and Bukovina
summary: That summer, the German army booted Russia out of Galicia and Bukovina, then pushed into Poland. The Russian press blamed Jews for the defeats, and the Russian military carried out pogroms as it retreated.

citation.quote: That summer, they were moving fast. The German army booted Russia out of Galicia and Bukovina, then kept going until they had pushed into Poland. The Russian press blamed Jews for the defeats, and the Russian military pogromed as it retreated.

title: Henryk Erlich joins Bund central committee
summary: Henryk Erlich rose through the party ranks and in 1915 became a member of the Bund's central committee while the Bund grew close to the Mensheviks.

citation.quote: Henryk was in and out of jail but rose through the ranks of the party and, in 1915, became a member of the Bund's central committee.

title: Bernard Goldstein attacks police commissioner in Siberia
summary: During a stint in Siberia in 1915, Bernard Goldstein slammed a kerosene lamp over the head of a police commissioner who had slapped him.

citation.quote: In 1915, during a stint in Siberia, Bernard earned his place in legend. During a routine checkup, the police commissioner flipped Bernard's eyelids up to check for trachoma... Not one to be insulted, Bernard slammed a kerosene lamp over the commissioner's head.

title: Medem sentenced to four years' hard labor
summary: Nearly two years after his arrest, the Warsaw judge sentenced Vladimir Medem to four years' hard labor in leg irons. With his kidney disease, Medem believed he would never leave prison alive.

citation.quote: In May 1915, nearly two years after his arrest, the Warsaw judge gave him a sentence. Four years' hard labor in leg irons.

title: Germans capture Warsaw; Medem freed
summary: On the night of August 4, the Russian army detonated mines on the bridges across the Vistula River as it fled Warsaw. The Germans entered the city and ordered the release of prisoners, including Vladimir Medem.

citation.quote: The night of August 4, pandemonium broke out. Gunfire. Cannon shriek. Medem, a revolutionary who plotted to bring down the state but who mostly wrote pamphlets, had never heard such fury in his life.

title: Sam Rothbort naturalized as white American
summary: On his naturalization papers, the official described Sam Rothbort as 'white,' marking his racial reclassification from 'Hebrew' upon entry.

citation.quote: In 1917, on his naturalization papers, the official merely described him as "white."

title: Sam Rothbort exhibits with Society of Brooklyn Artists
summary: Sam Rothbort first exhibited with the Society of Brooklyn Artists at the Abraham & Straus department store and at the Pouch Mansion in Prospect Heights.

citation.quote: That was the year he first exhibited with the Society of Brooklyn Artists in the glittery Abraham & Straus department store (a palace of commerce whose white-gloved attendants spoke twenty-three languages, from Gaelic to Arabic), and at the Pouch Mansion in Prospect Heights.

title: Siberian prisoners overthrow guards after March Revolution
summary: When the Revolution broke out in March 1917, Siberian prisoners overthrew their guards and presented the commissioner to Bernard Goldstein to execute, but Bernard refused.

citation.quote: When the Revolution broke out in March 1917, the prisoners overthrew their guards, tied the commissioner to a tree, and presented him to Bernard to execute. Bernard refused.

title: International Women's Day protests erupt in Petrograd
summary: On International Women's Day, working women of Petrograd took to the streets, starting in the Vyborgsky factory district and pouring into posh districts demanding bread and the death of the regime.

citation.quote: On the miserable gray morning of International Women's Day, March 8, 1917, working women of Petrograd took to the streets.

title: Over 200,000 on strike in Petrograd
summary: By March 11, more than two hundred thousand people were on strike in Petrograd. Stores shuttered, streetcars lay on their sides, and the air was filled with chants and gunfire.

citation.quote: By March 11, over two hundred thousand people were on strike. Stores shuttered. Streetcars lay on their sides, the windows smashed.

title: Pavlovsky Regiment mutinies; Petrograd Soviet formed
summary: The Fourth Company of the Pavlovsky Regiment mutinied, opening fire on mounted police; whole units began to defect. That afternoon, radicals in Tauride Palace declared the Temporary Executive Committee of the Soviet of Workers' and Soldiers' Deputies.

citation.quote: The next afternoon, the Fourth Company of the Imperial Guard's Pavlovsky Regiment mutinied. They marched out of their barracks, opened fire on a mounted police patrol, and disappeared into the streets.

title: Petrograd Soviet's first session at Tauride Palace
summary: Two hundred and fifty delegates gathered at Tauride Palace for the first session of the Petrograd Soviet, electing Menshevik Nikolai Chkheidze as president with Alexander Kerensky as vice president.

citation.quote: Two hundred and fifty people showed up. After hours of feverish chatter, they elected an old Georgian Menshevik named Nikolai Chkheidze as president of the Soviet, with the magnetic young Kerensky as a vice president.

title: Tsar Nicholas II abdicates
summary: On March 15, the tsar signed his abdication papers, ending 450 years of Romanov autocracy. News reached New York and Jewish neighborhoods flooded the streets in celebration.

citation.quote: On March 15, the tsar signed his abdication papers; with that, 450 years of autocracy were over.

title: First cabinet of Provisional Government appointed
summary: On the day of the tsar's abdication, the first cabinet of the Provisional Government of Revolutionary Russia was appointed. It abolished the death penalty, banned torture, granted women legal equality, and established free speech, free press, and universal suffrage.

citation.quote: On March 15, the day of the tsar's abdication, the first cabinet of the Provisional Government of Revolutionary Russia was appointed. Its members immediately set about trying to make Russia the freest country on earth.

title: Provisional government abolishes restrictions on Jews
summary: The provisional government announced the abolition of all restrictions based on nationality, religion, and class in the Russian Empire. After 126 years of oppression, Jews were officially equal.

citation.quote: On March 22, 1917, the provisional government announced the abolition of all restrictions based on nationality, religion, and class in the Russian Empire. After 126 years of government oppression, Jews were now officially equal.

title: Funeral for protesters at the Field of Mars
summary: Sophia Dubnova joined a million Petrograd residents at the Field of Mars for the funeral of protesters killed in the first days of the revolution. The Bund marched openly with its banner held high.

citation.quote: On March 23, she was one of the million Petrograd residents to make their way to the Field of Mars for the funeral of protesters killed in the first days of the revolution.

title: United States enters World War I
summary: America entered World War I in April 1917, after which it began to look less kindly on European Jewish radicals who opposed the conflict.

citation.quote: After America entered World War I in April 1917, it began to look less kindly on European Jewish radicals, many of whom opposed the conflict.

title: Lenin boards sealed train in Zurich
summary: Vladimir Lenin, joined by six Bundists and thirty-one other socialists, boarded a private train in Zurich and traveled through Germany with German government permission, en route to Petrograd.

citation.quote: On April 9, 1917, Vladimir Lenin, joined by six Bundists and thirty-one other socialists, boarded a private train in Zurich. They traveled through Germany, with the permission of the German government, to arrive in Petrograd on April 16.

title: Lenin arrives at Finland Station
summary: Lenin arrived in Petrograd at Finland Station, where Henryk Erlich and other Soviet delegates greeted him. Lenin turned his back on the delegation and from atop an armored car launched a denunciation of the Soviet.

citation.quote: They traveled through Germany, with the permission of the German government, to arrive in Petrograd on April 16. Though many in the Soviet viewed this trip through an enemy country as an act of treason, they knew Lenin from abroad and, more out of protocol than enthusiasm, organized a delegation to greet him.

title: Bund opens first legal conference inside Russia
summary: In Petrograd, the Bund opened the first conference it had ever legally held inside the Russian Empire. Mark Liber, recently returned from exile in Kazakhstan, had become a star orator and Menshevik leader.

citation.quote: On April 27, 1917, in Petrograd, the Bund opened the first conference it ever legally held inside the Russian Empire.

title: Sam Rothbort applies for American citizenship
summary: One month after the U.S. joined World War I, Samuel Rothbort, age 34, applied for American citizenship, renouncing his allegiance to any foreign power.

citation.quote: In May 1917, one month after the United States joined World War I, he finally applied for American citizenship. Samuel Rothbort, age thirty-four, renounced forever his allegiance to any foreign prince, potentate, state, or sovereign.

title: Espionage Act targets Jewish radicals
summary: The American government began targeting European Jewish radicals with the Espionage Act in June 1917.

citation.quote: The American government would target them with the Espionage Act that June.

title: Bund celebrates its twentieth birthday in Minsk
summary: With Warsaw and Vilna under German occupation, the Bund held its twentieth-anniversary jubilee in Minsk, home to its central committee and 3,500 local members.

citation.quote: On October 7, the Bund celebrated its twentieth birthday. With both Warsaw and Vilna under German occupation, the party chose Minsk, home to their central committee, to host their jubilee.

title: Bolshevik seizure of power in Petrograd
summary: Bolshevik detachments seized most strategic points in Petrograd, encircling the Winter Palace; Kerensky fled the city in a car flying the American Embassy's flag, and the pre-parliament was arrested.

citation.quote: There, he learned that the previous night, Bolshevik detachments had seized most strategic points in the city, even encircling the Winter Palace, the headquarters of the provisional government, which was meeting there that night. Kerensky had escaped the city in a car flying the American Embassy's flag.

title: Second Congress of Soviets opens at Smolny
summary: The Second Congress of Soviets opened with Fyodor Dan declaring the Winter Palace under siege; the Aurora fired on the palace as Bolsheviks and Left SRs took the presidium and Martov called for a socialist coalition government.

citation.quote: The Soviet's old chairman, the Menshevik Fyodor Dan, opened the congress with a declaration that the Winter Palace was under siege. He and the rest of the Soviet's former leaders left the stage, to be replaced by twenty-one Bolsheviks and Left SRs, including Leon Trotsky.

title: Erlich leads walkout from Second Congress of Soviets
summary: Henryk Erlich denounced the assault on the Winter Palace and led roughly fifty delegates of Mensheviks, Socialist Revolutionaries, and Bundists out of Smolny, leaving the floor to the Bolsheviks.

citation.quote: Erlich led fifty delegates toward the door. I doubt he realized he was giving in to the same tendency that the Bund had shown fourteen years before, when Medem and Liber walked out of the third conference of the RSDLP and left the floor clear for Lenin's takeover.

title: Constituent Assembly elections begin
summary: Voting for the Russian Constituent Assembly began and stretched over two weeks. Bund candidates Abramovich and Frumkin lost their races, leaving the Bund with a single delegate.

citation.quote: Voting began on November 25 and stretched over two weeks. Abramovich and Frumkin lost their races. All the Bund had to show for themselves was a single delegate.

title: Poland reunited and independent under Pilsudski
summary: After 130 years of partition, Poland stood united and independent under the leadership of Józef Pilsudski; by 1918 he was no longer the fiery leftist of his youth.

citation.quote: After 130 years of partition, Poland stood united and independent under the leadership of general Józef Pilsudski, aristocrat, revolutionary bank robber, war hero, and longtime acquaintance of the Bund... By 1918, Pilsudski was no longer the fiery leftist of his youth.

title: Kyiv uprising against Hetman Skoropadskyi
summary: Days after the end of World War I, posters in Kyiv called for overthrow of Hetman Skoropadskyi and restoration of the Ukrainian People's Republic; Bernard Goldstein led Bundist fighters in the 1918 uprising.

citation.quote: Days after the end of World War I, posters went up around Kyiv calling on the population to overthrow the hated regime of Hetman Skoropadskyi and to restore the Ukrainian People's Republic... When the 1918 uprising against the hetman began, Bernard's two hundred fighters took over the elegant streets around the Bessarabian Market.

title: Approximately 200,000 Jews murdered in pogroms
summary: Around two hundred thousand Jews were murdered in the pogroms between 1918 and 1921, and six hundred thousand more fled to Western Europe, America, and Palestine.

citation.quote: Around two hundred thousand Jews were murdered in the pogroms that took place between 1918 and 1921. The chaos forced six hundred thousand more to flee to Western Europe, America, and Palestine.

title: Medem predicts Bolshevik terror will turn inward
summary: Vladimir Medem predicted that the terror Bolsheviks wielded against their rivals would soon turn inward, foretelling revolutionary tribunals among the Bolsheviks themselves.

citation.quote: In 1918, he predicted that the terror Bolsheviks wielded against their rivals would soon turn inward, to be used against each other.

title: Musa Kazim al-Husseini appointed mayor of Jerusalem
summary: The British appointed Musa Kazim Pasha al-Husseini as mayor of Jerusalem.

citation.quote: In 1918, the British had appointed him as mayor of Jerusalem, only to fire him in 1921 after he delivered a passionate speech at the anti-occupation riots that broke out at the city's Nabi Musa festival.

title: Constituent Assembly convenes in Petrograd
summary: Over four hundred delegates converged on Tauride Palace for the long-awaited Constituent Assembly. The Bolsheviks encircled the building with Red Guards and forced the delegates out at gunpoint after a single session.
