citation.quote: On January 18, 1918, came the long-awaited day of the Constituent Assembly. Inside Tauride Palace, over four hundred delegates, from Irkutsk to Tiflis, converged to decide the most important questions of their revolutionary homeland.

title: Bolshevik forces fire on pro-Assembly march
summary: Tens of thousands of workers and intellectuals marched in the Field of Mars in support of the Constituent Assembly. Bolshevik forces opened fire, killing twenty-one people.

citation.quote: Bolshevik forces killed twenty-one people that day.

title: Ukrainian Central Rada declares independence
summary: After the Bolshevik dispersal of the Constituent Assembly, the Ukrainian Central Rada declared Ukrainian independence. Its leaders had wrangled for autonomy for a year only to be dismissed by Russia.

citation.quote: If the Bolsheviks would shut down the most cherished organ of revolutionary democracy, Vynnychenko wrote, then they were "the same Russian chauvinists and imperialists" as the last regime. On January 22, 1918, the Rada declared Ukrainian independence.

title: Kyiv arsenal uprising and Podil pogrom
summary: Hundreds of pro-Bolshevik workers, some of them Jewish, launched an uprising at Kyiv's arsenal. Petliura's Haidamaks crushed the rebellion and slaughtered twenty-two Jews in the Podil neighborhood.

citation.quote: Five days after the Rada declared independence, Russian soldiers laid siege to Kyiv, and on January 29, hundreds of pro-Bolshevik workers launched an uprising at the city's arsenal... They slaughtered twenty-two Jews, two of them Bundists.

title: Russians take Kyiv
summary: Russian forces captured Kyiv. Local Bundist leadership condemned the Russians as an occupation army and refused to recognize the Bolshevik government.

citation.quote: Petliura's victory was short-lived. On February 9, the Russians took Kyiv.

title: Ukraine signs defense treaty with Central Powers
summary: Desperate to free themselves from Russian invaders, Ukraine's leaders signed a defense treaty with Germany and Austria. Three weeks later, Haidamaks and Germans expelled the Reds from Kyiv.

citation.quote: Desperate to free themselves from their Russian invaders, on February 9, Ukraine's leaders signed a defense treaty with Germany and Austria. Three weeks later, Haidamaks and their German backers booted the Reds from Kyiv.

title: Treaty of Brest-Litovsk signed
summary: The Bolsheviks signed a treaty with Germany and Austria at Brest-Litovsk, ending Russia's role in World War I. Russia gave up most of the former Pale of Settlement and over half of its industrial land.

citation.quote: On March 3, after months of wrangling, the Bolsheviks signed their own treaty with Germany and Austria in the city of Brest-Litovsk, ending Russia's role in World War I.

title: Germans arrest the Ukrainian Rada
summary: As Rada delegates gathered at Kyiv's Pedagogical Lyceum to discuss German rule, a German officer burst in and put the entire government under arrest.

citation.quote: On the afternoon of April 28, Rada delegates gathered in their headquarters at Kyiv's Pedagogical Lyceum to discuss the increasingly tyrannical German rule. Rafes had just started to speak when a German officer burst in, barked that the building was surrounded, and put the entire government under arrest.

title: Erlich attends Menshevik conference in Moscow
summary: Henryk Erlich went to Moscow to represent the Bund at a Menshevik conference, where the party debated whether to keep running candidates for soviets or join armed anti-Bolshevik uprisings.

citation.quote: In May, Erlich went to Moscow to represent the Bund at a Menshevik conference. The party was more divided than ever, unsure if they should keep running candidates for the soviets, despite repression, or forgo what Liber called "Bonapartist clubs that gather together around these déclassé dregs" and instead join armed anti-Bolshevik uprisings.

title: Menshevik report documents socialist persecution in Minsk
summary: A Menshevik report noted that in Minsk the persecution of socialists had reached such proportions that they had to go underground, just like under czarism.

citation.quote: A Menshevik report in June 1918 noted that in Minsk, "the persecution of socialists has reached such proportions that they had to go underground, just like under czarism."

title: Sophia Dubnova and Henryk Erlich leave Russia for Lublin
summary: When their travel permits arrived, Sophia and Henryk took their starving sons by freight train west toward Henryk's Polish hometown of Lublin, then under Austrian occupation.

citation.quote: When their travel permits arrived that August, Henryk and Sophia swore that the move would not be final. They would stay in Lublin just long enough for their sons to put on weight, then resume their lives in Petrograd.

title: Slacker raids in immigrant neighborhoods
summary: During the 'slacker raids' of September 1918, de Woodey's officers and the American Protective League herded sixty thousand men without draft cards to the Fifth Avenue Armory.

citation.quote: He made his career persecuting Wobblies, Indian freedom fighters, and a famous Turkish dancing girl, but his path crossed Sam's during the "slacker raids" of September 1918.

title: Sam Rothbort registered for draft at Local Board 75
summary: Fourteen years after escaping conscription into the tsarist army, Sam Rothbort was registered at Local Board 75 in Greenpoint to fight in World War I.

citation.quote: So it was that on September 12, 1918, fourteen years after he escaped conscription into the tsarist army, Sam stood at Local Board 75 in Greenpoint, to be registered to fight in someone else's war.

title: Ukrainian fighters declare Lviv capital of West Ukrainian People's Republic
summary: After the Germans left in November 1918, Ukrainian fighters declared Lviv the capital of their short-lived West Ukrainian People's Republic.

citation.quote: After the Germans left in November 1918, Ukrainian fighters declared Lviv the capital of their short-lived West Ukrainian People's Republic.

title: Lviv pogrom by Polish army
summary: When Polish troops took Lviv, soldiers burned Jewish neighborhoods, raped women, and murdered at least seventy-three Jews in a massacre carried out by a professional army.

citation.quote: When Polish troops took Lviv (or was it Lwow?), Lemberg was the place that suffered... The Polish army murdered at least seventy-three Jews. When Jewish newspapers reported on the pogrom, the Polish government blamed the victims.

title: Pogrom wave across former Pale of Settlement
summary: Over a thousand pogroms took place between November 1918 and March 1921 within the former Pale of Settlement, of unprecedented ferocity and sadism.

citation.quote: The Lviv massacre was the among the first of over a thousand pogroms that took place between November 1918 and March 1921 within the former Pale of Settlement. They were of a ferocity and sadism never before experienced in eastern Europe.

title: Germany signs World War I armistice
summary: On November 11, 1918, the Republic of Germany signed an armistice, ending the First World War before America could send Sam Rothbort to fight.

citation.quote: On November 11, 1918, the Republic of Germany signed an armistice. The First World War ended before America could send Sam Rothbort to fight.

title: Vynnychenko's Directorate returns to power in Kyiv
summary: In late December 1918, Vynnychenko and his Directorate returned to power in Kyiv with help from the Bund, offering promises of autonomy and condemnations of pogroms.

citation.quote: In late December, Vynnychenko and his Directorate returned to power in Kyiv, with a little bit of help from the Bund.

title: Pedro Wald arrested in Argentina
summary: Argentine police arrested Bundist Pedro Wald, accusing him of attempting to overthrow the government and form a Patagonian Soviet Republic.

citation.quote: One issue might contain a dispatch from their comrade Pedro Wald in Buenos Aires. (In 1919, Argentine police arrested Wald on accusations of attempting to overthrow the government and form a Patagonian Soviet Republic.)

title: Soviet Russia founds the Comintern
summary: Soviet Russia announced the creation of the Communist International (Comintern), intended to replace the discredited Second International and unite socialist parties worldwide.

citation.quote: The same questions that split the Russian Bund threatened to tear the Polish Bund apart when, in 1919, Soviet Russia announced the creation of the Communist International, or Comintern, an international organization of labor parties intended to replace the discredited Second International.

title: Sam Rothbort finds patron Hamilton Easter Field
summary: Sam Rothbort finally found a patron in art critic and collector Hamilton Easter Field, who championed his work and hung his paintings at home exhibitions.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: In 1919, Sam Rothbort finally found a patron: Hamilton Easter Field.

title: Endeks win plurality in Polish elections
summary: In parliamentary elections in January 1919, the Endeks won a plurality of the vote.

citation.quote: In parliamentary elections later that month, Endeks won a plurality of the vote.

title: Berdichev pogrom
summary: When pogromists gathered outside Bundist mayor David Lipetz's house in January 1919 demanding 'the Yid who runs this city,' they murdered seventeen Jews that day, then attacked the funeral and killed two more.

citation.quote: Yet, when pogromists gathered outside his house in January screaming, "Give us the Yid who runs this city," he was as helpless as any old-time shtetl victim... Pogromists murdered seventeen Jews that day.

title: Endek coup attempt in Poland
summary: On January 4, 1919, the racist Endek party tried to overthrow the Polish government. The coup failed, but Pilsudski refused to charge the conspirators.

citation.quote: Poland began 1919 in turmoil. On January 4, the racist Endek party tried to overthrow the government. The coup failed, but Pilsudski refused to charge the conspirators, afraid this would make them martyrs.

title: Petliura takes over the Directorate
summary: The pogrom wave grew after Petliura took over the Directorate in February 1919.

citation.quote: The pogrom wave grew after Petliura took over the Directorate in February.

title: Proskurov pogrom
summary: A few days after Petliura took over the Directorate, troops led by Ivan Semesenko rode through Proskurov and murdered 1,500 people in Petliura's name.

citation.quote: A few days later, a division of Petliura's troops led by Ivan Semesenko rode their horses through the main drag of the small town of Proskurov and murdered 1,500 people in Petliura's name.

title: Moishe Rafes founds the Kombund in Kyiv
summary: In February 1919, in Kyiv, Moishe Rafes inaugurated the Communist Bund (Kombund), which would ally with the Red Army as the only force seen capable of protecting Jewish workers.

citation.quote: In February 1919, in Kyiv, Moishe Rafes inaugurated a new group, the Communist Bund, or Kombund. (The Bolsheviks had changed their name to the Communist Party a year before.)

title: Polish army takes Volkovysk
summary: The Polish army took Volkovysk in February 1919, and the town had been in bad straits ever since.

citation.quote: The Polish army took Volkovysk in February 1919, and the town had been in bad straits ever since.

title: Erlich denounces pogroms to Warsaw Soviet
summary: In March 1919, Henryk Erlich told the Warsaw Soviet that reactionary forces had organized anti-Jewish pogroms to deflect attention from real needs and drown the revolutionary struggle.

citation.quote: "In order to deflect the attention of the masses from their real needs, and to drown the revolutionary struggle of the proletariat in a wave of race-hatred…the reactionary forces organized a series of anti-Jewish pogroms," Erlich told the Warsaw Soviet in March.

title: Pinsk massacre
summary: In early April 1919, the Polish army arrested thirty-five Jews at an aid distribution meeting in Pinsk and gunned them down against a monastery wall, including Bundists Moishe Glauberman and Abraham Chaim Haltsman.

citation.quote: In early April, in Pinsk, the Polish army arrested thirty-five Jews at a meeting about aid distribution and gunned them down against the wall of a nearby monastery. Two victims were Bundists: the municipal worker Moishe Glauberman and the teacher Abraham Chaim Haltsman.

title: Pilsudski takes Vilna; eighty-five Jews murdered
summary: On April 19, 1919, Pilsudski led Polish forces into Vilna, and in the days that followed his soldiers murdered eighty-five Jews, including playwright A. Vayter.

citation.quote: On April 19, Pilsudski led Polish forces into Vilna. In the days that followed, his soldiers murdered eighty-five Jews.

title: Sarah Fuchs interrogated by Cheka; takes her own life
summary: In June 1919, the Cheka stormed Berdichev's Bundist cultural club and interrogated Sarah Fuchs for 24 hours, after which she traveled to Kyiv and drowned herself in the Dnipro.

citation.quote: In June 1919, the Cheka stormed Berdichev's Bundist cultural club, where Fuchs spent much of her time. "Where is the counterrevolutionary Sarah Fuchs?" one agent demanded. "I am the counterrevolutionary Sarah Fuchs," she replied.

title: Ben-Gurion elected secretary general of the Histadrut
summary: David Ben-Gurion was elected secretary general of the Histadrut, a Jewish-only labor union that locked Palestinians out of the Zionist economy.

citation.quote: In 1920, Ben-Gurion was elected secretary general of the Histadrut, a Jewish-only labor union that locked Palestinians out of the Zionist economy in the same way Polish labor policy locked Jews out of jobs in Warsaw.

title: Bund's twelfth congress in Gomel splits the party
summary: At the Bund's twelfth congress in Gomel in April 1920, a majority led by Esther Frumkin voted to enter the Communist Party, prompting Raphael Abramovich to form the Social Democratic Bund.

citation.quote: In April 1920, at the Bund's twelfth congress, in Gomel, the disagreements between the party's pro- and anti-Soviet factions led to a final rupture. A majority of delegates, led by Esther Frumkin, voted to have the Bund enter the Communist Party as an autonomous organization.

title: Volkovysk pogrom over blood libel
summary: In April 1920, after rumors spread about matzoh made with babies' blood, soldiers smashed up the Jewish neighborhood of Volkovysk.

citation.quote: In April 1920, after rumors spread about matzoh made with babies' blood, soldiers smashed up the Jewish neighborhood.

title: Bund's Krakow convention votes to join Comintern
summary: At the Bund's Krakow convention, a majority of delegates voted to join the Comintern. Vladimir Medem was the main dissenter.

citation.quote: In April 1920, at the Bund's Krakow convention, a majority of delegates voted to join the Comintern. The main dissenter was Vladimir Medem.

title: Poland takes Kyiv with Petliura's help
summary: In May 1920, with Petliura's help, Poland took Kyiv and Pilsudski returned to Warsaw as a hero.

citation.quote: That month, with Petliura's help, Poland took Kyiv and Pilsudski returned to Warsaw as a hero.

title: Police beat May Day celebrants in Warsaw
summary: On May Day 1920, after Medem spoke before twenty thousand people in Iron Gate Square, police sealed the side streets and beat the celebrants. Cops also wrecked the Bund's club in Praga.

citation.quote: On May Day of 1920, after Medem spoke before twenty thousand people in Iron Gate Square, police sealed the side streets and beat the celebrants to a pulp.

title: Erlich demands peace at Warsaw city council
summary: On July 8, 1920, at an emergency meeting of the Warsaw city council, Henryk Erlich demanded immediate peace and an end to Polish imperial ambitions. The government later banned the party.

citation.quote: On July 8, 1920, at an emergency meeting of the Warsaw city council, Henryk Erlich demanded immediate peace and an end to Polish imperial ambitions. "What are we fighting for?" he asked. "Land which doesn't belong to us."

title: Polish counterattack at Izabelin
summary: On August 15, 1920, Polish forces counterattacked at Izabelin, forcing the Soviets into a shambolic retreat. Polish soldiers then carried out pogroms wherever they went.

citation.quote: Then, on August 15, Polish forces counterattacked in a little town called Izabelin, forcing the Soviets into a shambolic retreat. Wherever the Polish army went, soldiers carried out pogroms to avenge themselves upon the Jews who they believed were traitors.

title: Police arrest Henryk Erlich
summary: The police caught Henryk Erlich in September 1920 after he shaved off his beard and went for a walk; cops grabbed him within minutes.

citation.quote: The police caught Henryk Erlich in September. Bored with hiding at his friend's place, he shaved off his signature beard in a half-assed effort to conceal his identity and went for a walk. Cops grabbed him within minutes.

title: Polish army retakes Volkovysk
summary: In October 1920, the Polish army invaded and retook Volkovysk; the rabbi paid off the army with New York cash to stop a threatened slaughter of the Jewish population.

citation.quote: In October 1920, the Polish army invaded, retook, liberated, and/or occupied Volkovysk. When a well-known captain died in the battle, the Poles announced they would retaliate by slaughtering the entire Jewish population.

title: Poland and Soviet Russia sign ceasefire
summary: Poland and Soviet Russia signed a ceasefire agreement in October 1920, though official peace would have to wait till the Treaty of Riga the following spring.

citation.quote: Poland and Soviet Russia signed a ceasefire agreement in October 1920, though official peace would have to wait till the Treaty of Riga the following spring.

title: Henryk Erlich released from prison
summary: Henryk Erlich was released from prison in November 1920, thinner and with stubble on his sallow face. Other Bundists trickled out of jails and concentration camps.

citation.quote: They released Erlich from prison in November. He was thinner, Sophia wrote, "with little tufts of stubble on his sallow face." Other Bundists trickled out of the jails and concentration camps.

title: Moyshe Olgin visits Moscow
summary: Bundist writer Moyshe Olgin visited Moscow and watched the old tsarist general Aleksei Brusilov salute Jewish Bundist David Petrovsky at a Red Square military parade, an image that converted him to communism.

citation.quote: When Bundist writer Moyshe Olgin visited Moscow in 1921, he watched the old tsarist general Aleksei Brusilov salute Petrovsky at a military parade in Red Square.

title: Russian Bund liquidated by Soviet order
summary: While the Polish Bund's secret envoy X traveled to Moscow, the Soviet government ordered the Russian Bund's liquidation. Hundreds gathered in Minsk to hear the Russian Bundists' final speeches before voting to dissolve the party.

citation.quote: While still in transit, he received a telegram from the Russian Bund to let him know that the Soviet government had ordered the party's liquidation. As soon as he arrived in Moscow, he got on a train to Minsk to watch their funeral.

title: Alter and Wasser plead at Third Comintern Congress
summary: The Bund sent Chaim Wasser and Viktor Alter to plead their case at the Third Comintern Congress in Moscow, where they received a chilly reception from the Jewish Section.

citation.quote: Clinging to hope, the Bund sent two local leaders, Chaim Wasser and Viktor Alter, to plead their case at the Third Comintern Congress in Moscow.

title: U.S. Emergency Quota Act passed
summary: A few months after Medem's arrival in America, Congress passed the Emergency Quota Act, radically slashing immigration from the Middle East and eastern and southern Europe, targeting Jews.

citation.quote: A few months after his arrival, Congress passed the Emergency Quota Act, which radically slashed immigration from the Middle East and from eastern and southern Europe.

title: Musa Kazim fired as mayor of Jerusalem
summary: The British fired Musa Kazim Pasha al-Husseini as mayor of Jerusalem after he delivered a passionate speech at the anti-occupation riots at the Nabi Musa festival.

citation.quote: In 1918, the British had appointed him as mayor of Jerusalem, only to fire him in 1921 after he delivered a passionate speech at the anti-occupation riots that broke out at the city's Nabi Musa festival.

title: Vladimir and Gina Medem arrive at Ellis Island
summary: After failing to convince Bund comrades to reject Comintern alignment, Medem resigned from the central committee and emigrated with Gina to New York, arriving at Ellis Island.

citation.quote: He and Gina arrived at Ellis Island in January 1921. He would never see Poland again.

title: Bund rejects the Twenty-One Conditions in Danzig
summary: At an underground conference in the Free City of Danzig, Bundists voted to reject the Comintern's Twenty-One Conditions, ending their courtship with the Comintern. A splinter sect of Soviet sympathizers quit the party.

citation.quote: In December 1921, at an underground conference held in the Free City of Danzig, Bundists voted to reject the Twenty-One Conditions. A splinter sect of Soviet fanboys flounced out and quit the party.

title: Bund's first parliamentary election campaign in Poland
summary: The Bund plunged into their first ever election campaign for the Polish parliament, offering a social-democratic platform. The Left split between PPS, Bund, and communists; the Bund won no seats while Endeks took 40 percent.

citation.quote: In the autumn of 1922, the Bund plunged into their first ever election campaign for the parliament in Poland.

title: Gabriel Narutowicz assassinated
summary: Liberal populist Gabriel Narutowicz was elected president of Poland thanks in part to Jewish votes, sparking nationalist riots. A few days later, a nationalist painter shot Narutowicz dead at an art exhibition.

citation.quote: On inauguration day, rioters barricaded Ujazdów Avenue, pelted Narutowicz's carriage with snowballs, and beat leftists, journalists, and Jews. A few days later, a nationalist painter shot Narutowicz dead at an art exhibition.

title: Musa Kazim writes to British occupiers protesting immigration
summary: Musa Kazim wrote a letter to Palestine's British occupiers protesting that immigrants were entering Palestine by the might of England against the will of the people.

citation.quote: "The immigrants dumped upon the country from different parts of the world are ignorant of the language, customs and character of the Arabs and enter Palestine by the might of England against the will of the people," he wrote in a 1922 letter to Palestine's British occupiers.

title: Bund launches Saturday edition of Folkstsaytung
summary: The Bund decided to publish a Saturday edition of Folkstsaytung, deliberately flouting Sabbath rules and beginning a struggle with Orthodox Jews.

citation.quote: The Bund's struggle with Orthodox Jews began in 1922, when the party decided to publish a Saturday edition of Folkstsaytung, deliberately flouting rules that forbade work on the Sabbath and infuriating religious Jews.

title: Death of Hamilton Easter Field
summary: Hamilton Easter Field died of pneumonia at age forty-nine, ending the patronage that had launched Sam Rothbort into Brooklyn's High Art world.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: Or that's how it should have gone, but on April 10, 1922, Field died of pneumonia. He was only forty-nine.

title: Social Democratic Bund issues final bulletin
summary: After Cheka arrests of Bundist leaders across Russia, the Social Democratic Bund issued its last illegal bulletin in 1923. After that, silence.

citation.quote: More arrests of Bundist leaders across Russia followed. The Social Democratic Bund issued its last illegal bulletin in 1923. After that, silence.

title: Jabotinsky publishes "The Iron Wall"
summary: Vladimir Jabotinsky wrote an essay called "The Iron Wall" arguing that Israel, like all colonies, could only be built by subjugating the native people.

citation.quote: In 1923, he wrote an essay called "The Iron Wall" that shattered the genteel doublespeak of the Zionist Congress. In it he said that, like all colonies, Israel could only be built by subjugating the native people.

title: Death of Vladimir Medem
summary: Vladimir Medem died of nephritis in Brooklyn at the age of forty-four. Despite a snowstorm, ten thousand people came to his funeral.

citation.quote: Medem died of nephritis on January 9, 1923, in Brooklyn, at the age of fourty-four. Despite the snowstorm, ten thousand people came to his funeral.

title: Bund May Day procession battles in Theater Square
summary: On May Day 1923, the Bund organized a massive procession flanked by a thousand militiamen. Fighting erupted in Theater Square between Bundists, nationalists, communists, and police; Bernard Goldstein saved the Bund's banner by hiding it under his shirt.

citation.quote: On May Day 1923, the Bund organized a massive procession, flanked by a thousand militiamen holding wooden bats. The marchers wove their way to Theater Square, where the Polish Socialist Party had saved them a spot.

title: Wladyslaw Grabski becomes prime minister of Poland
summary: Endek economist Wladyslaw Grabski became prime minister of Poland with near-dictatorial powers granted by parliament, beginning austerity measures that devastated workers and Jews.

citation.quote: On December 23, 1923, Endek economist Wladyslaw Grabski became prime minister of Poland. Granted near-dictatorial powers by parliament, Grabski immediately began to slash and burn.

title: Viktor Alter travels to Palestine
summary: Viktor Alter sailed for Jaffa to see the Zionist endeavor up close, later chronicling the trip in his pamphlet The Truth About Palestine.

citation.quote: In 1924, Viktor Alter sailed for Jaffa to see the Zionist endeavor up close. He chronicled the trip in The Truth About Palestine, a pamphlet he published upon his return to Warsaw.

title: Sam Rothbort moves family to Uniondale farm
summary: Embittered by his cold reception in New York art circles, Sam Rothbort moved his family to two acres in Uniondale on Long Island, where he set up a no-kill egg farm.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: In 1924, he moved the family to two acres of land in Uniondale on Long Island, where he set up a no-kill egg farm.

title: Max Weinreich founds YIVO Institute in Vilna
summary: The Bundist Max Weinreich founded the YIVO Institute for Jewish Research in Vilna to study the culture of eastern European Jews.

citation.quote: In 1925, the Bundist Max Weinreich founded the YIVO Institute for Jewish Research in Vilna to study the culture of eastern European Jews.

title: Sam Rothbort takes up sculpture
summary: In Uniondale, Sam Rothbort took up the hammer and chisel, sculpting reliefs from fieldstone and scavenged fenceposts that depicted pogrom victims and biblical prophets.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: In 1925, he took up the hammer and chisel. He preferred fieldstone and scavenged fenceposts, battered materials that hid stories.

title: Poland enters major economic depression
summary: By 1926, Grabski's reforms had failed and Poland was in a major economic depression, with a third of the workforce unemployed.

citation.quote: Grabski's reforms didn't work, and by 1926, Poland was in a major economic depression, with a third of the workforce unemployed.

title: Bund founds SKIF, the Socialist Children's Union
summary: The Bund created SKIF, the Socialist Children's Union, to raise the next generation of working-class Jewish kids in Poland.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: In 1926, the same year as Pilsudski's coup, the Bund created SKIF, the Socialist Children's Union.

title: Bund founds Morgenstern sports club
summary: The same year as Pilsudski's coup, the Bund founded their sports club, Morgenstern, which organized hikes, gymnastics, boxing, swimming, and soccer tournaments.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: The same year, the Bund founded their sports club, Morgenstern.

title: Bund opens Medem Sanatorium in Miedzeszyn
summary: The Bund opened the Medem Sanatorium on four acres of forest in Miedzeszyn, near Warsaw, for poor children at risk of tuberculosis, directed by Shloyme Gilinsky.

citation.quote: In January 1926, the Bund opened the crown jewel of their network: the Medem Sanatorium, built on four acres of forest in Miedzeszyn, near Warsaw, for poor children at risk of tuberculosis, and named after their legendary leader.

title: Pilsudski's coup in Poland
summary: Józef Pilsudski overthrew the Polish government, marching troops over the Kierbedz Bridge into Warsaw and seizing key points of the city.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: On May 12, 1926, the Bund's leaders woke up to the news that Józef Pilsudski was overthrowing the Polish government.

title: Folkstsaytung renamed Naye Folkstsaytung
summary: The Bund's Yiddish newspaper Folkstsaytung changed its name to Naye Folkstsaytung.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: Folkstsaytung changed its name to Naye [New] Folkstsaytung in 1927.

title: Morgenstern mass acrobatic display in Warsaw
summary: Morgenstern took over a Warsaw circus for a mass acrobatic display featuring hundreds of gymnasts and a parade of distinct age-group uniforms.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: In April 1927, Morgenstern took over a Warsaw circus for a mass acrobatic display. Hundreds of gymnasts performed.

title: Bund celebrates thirtieth anniversary
summary: The Bund celebrated their thirtieth anniversary in the largest hall in Jewish Warsaw, with Henryk Erlich delivering the centerpiece speech.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: In October, the Bund celebrated their thirtieth anniversary in the largest hall in Jewish Warsaw.

title: Stalin expels Trotsky and banishes him to Kazakhstan
summary: Stalin's party expelled Trotsky and banished him to a remote backwater in Kazakhstan, nearly four years after Lenin's death.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: Lenin was nearly four years dead in November 1927 when his party, now helmed by the former bank robber Joseph Stalin, expelled Trotsky and banished him to a remote backwater in Kazakhstan.

title: Jabotinsky returns to Palestine to set up newspaper
summary: Jabotinsky returned to Palestine in 1928 to set up a newspaper and took up Zionist calls to buy and bulldoze adjoining Muslim homes near the Wailing Wall.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: When Jabotinsky returned to Palestine in 1928 to set up a newspaper, he took up Zionist calls to buy and bulldoze adjoining Muslim homes.

title: Seventh Palestine Arab Congress in Jerusalem
summary: Naye Folkstsaytung covered the seventh Palestine Arab Congress in Jerusalem, which demanded a democratic parliament, an end to the British occupation, and a halt on Zionist immigration.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: In 1928, Naye Folkstsaytung covered the seventh Palestine Arab Congress in Jerusalem, which demanded a democratic parliament, an end to the British occupation, and a halt on Zionist immigration.

title: Comintern announces social fascism doctrine
summary: At the Comintern's sixth world congress, Stalin announced a new theory called social fascism, declaring democratic socialist parties to be as bad as real fascists.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: At the Comintern's sixth world congress, which closed in September 1928, Stalin announced a new theory called social fascism.

title: Wailing Wall riots and Hebron massacre
summary: Following Zionist provocations on Tisha b'Av, ten days of communal violence broke out in Palestine; the most notorious massacre saw a Palestinian mob murder sixty-seven Jews in Hebron.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: After a year of stupid squabbles, tit-for-tat dick waving, and identitarian provocation, things finally exploded in 1929, when, on the Jewish mourning day of Tisha b'Av, thousands of Jabotinsky's followers raised the Zionist movement's flag and chanted that the wall was theirs.

title: Bundist speakers tour Poland on Palestine
summary: Bundist speakers toured Poland, giving hundreds of lectures on Palestinians, Zionism, and the British Mandate; G. Zeibert later traveled to New York to denounce mass hysteria over the riots.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: In 1929, Bundist speakers toured Poland, giving hundreds of lectures on Palestinians, Zionism, and the British Mandate.

title: American stock market crash devastates Polish economy
summary: After the American stock market crashed in the fall of 1929, the reverberations devastated the Polish economy.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: After the American stock market crashed in the fall of 1929, the reverberations devastated the Polish economy.

title: Betar's first international conference in Warsaw
summary: Hundreds of young Jews in brown military shirts marched to the Great Synagogue on Tlomackie Street for the first international conference of Vladimir Jabotinsky's Betar youth movement.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: On New Year's Day 1929, Warsaw watched with astonishment as hundreds of young Jews clad in brown military shirts marched to the Great Synagogue on Tlomackie Street for the first international conference of Vladimir Jabotinsky's Betar youth movement.

title: Hoover slashes US immigration quotas
summary: Herbert Hoover radically slashed immigration quotas and instructed American consulates to issue no more than 10 percent of the meager number of visas allotted to each country.

citation.quote: In 1930, Herbert Hoover had radically slashed immigration quotas, then instructed American consulates to issue no more than 10 percent of the meager number of visas allotted to each country.

title: Krakow opposition bloc and Pilsudski's crackdown
summary: Center and left parties met in Krakow to form a new electoral bloc against Pilsudski; he responded by dissolving parliament and throwing fifteen opposition deputies into a concentration camp.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: Bristling under Pilsudski's authoritarianism, in June 1930, center and left parties met in Krakow to form a new electoral bloc to oppose the country's descent into dictatorship.

title: PPS and Bund hold joint May Day parade
summary: In 1931, the Polish Socialist Party and the Bund marched together for the first time in a joint May Day parade.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: In 1931, the two parties marched together for the first time in a joint May Day parade.

title: Congress of Labor and Socialist International in Vienna
summary: After the 1931 olympiad, the Congress of the Labor and Socialist International opened in Vienna; Henryk Erlich gave a speech warning the German Social Democrats about the rise of fascism.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: World disarmament and general peace were the themes of the Congress of the Labor and Socialist International, a grouping of democratic socialist parties that the Bund had joined two years before, and which opened in Vienna right after the 1931 olympiad.

title: Nationalist riots at Polish universities
summary: Young nationalist rioters expelled their Jewish classmates at Krakow University and the University of Warsaw, sparking nationwide riots that forced the government to shutter every college in Warsaw.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: It started that fall semester at the Krakow University, where young nationalist rioters expelled their Jewish classmates.

title: Morgenstern athletes head to Vienna Workers' Olympiad
summary: Three hundred athletes from the Bundist sports club Morgenstern prepared to leave for the third Workers' Olympiad in Vienna, organized by the Socialist Workers' Sport International.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: In July 1931, three hundred athletes from the Bundist sports club Morgenstern prepared to leave for the third Workers' Olympiad in Vienna.

title: Sophia Dubnova visits Nazi-era Berlin
summary: Sophia Dubnova took her son Victor to visit her parents in Berlin, finding a city transformed by Brownshirt violence and political clashes that had left over a hundred people dead by mid-July.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: In the summer of 1932, Sophia Dubnova took her son Victor to visit her parents in Berlin.

title: Nazis become largest party in Reichstag
summary: After the July elections, the Nazis became the largest party in the Reichstag, following Brownshirt street violence and the social democrats' refusal to call a general strike.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: After the July elections, the Nazis were the largest party in the Reichstag.

title: Bund archives smuggled from Berlin to Paris
summary: After Nazi storm troopers occupied the Bund's archive site at 68 Lindenstrasse, Franz Kursky smuggled the documents out via a secret side door; Leon Blum arranged for Paris's Bibliotheque Nationale to purchase the collection.

citation.quote: But in 1933, he was a paranoid fifty-nine, and these were times of terror. Storm troopers made the laws.

title: US accepts under 2,000 German immigrants
summary: In 1933, the United States accepted less than two thousand immigrants from Germany under Hoover's restrictive policy, which was supported by the American Federation of Labor.

citation.quote: In 1933, the United States accepted less than two thousand immigrants from Germany.

title: British police kill Musa Kazim Pasha
summary: British police beat Musa Kazim Pasha to death at a protest in Jerusalem in 1933, after his efforts had failed to gain Palestinians political rights or stop Zionist land purchases.

citation.quote: As if to underscore their indifference to Palestinian opinion, British police beat Musa Kazim Pasha to death in 1933 at a protest in Jerusalem.

title: Hindenburg appoints Hitler chancellor of Germany
summary: At the end of January 1933, Hindenburg appointed Hitler the chancellor of Germany. The social democrats declined to act, and the communists refused to work with them.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: At the end of January, Hindenburg appointed Hitler the chancellor of Germany.

title: Reichstag fire in Berlin
summary: One month after Hitler's appointment, the Reichstag was set on fire, with smoke and a red-stained sky visible from the Bund Archives in Berlin.

citation.chapter: Chapter 17: Here Where We Live Is Our Country
citation.quote: One month after Hitler's appointment, on February 27, the crew at the Bund Archives in Berlin would have found their evening interrupted by the smell of smoke.

title: Reichstag fire and Nazi crackdown
summary: After the Reichstag fire, Hitler convinced Hindenburg to suspend civil liberties; police banned the leftist press and arrested hundreds of communists and social democrats.

citation.quote: On the night of February 28, when Naye Folkstsaytung's anonymous Berlin correspondent telegraphed his copy to Warsaw, he must have known that a fundamental rupture had taken place between the future and the past. He had seen the Reichstag's glass dome shatter.

title: Naras attack Warsaw Jews in single night
summary: In a single night in 1934, Nara militants wounded thirty people in a raid on a Jewish library in Warsaw and beat to death a Bundist battle squad leader on the other side of the city.

citation.quote: In a single night in 1934, Naras wounded thirty people in a raid on a Jewish library on one side of Warsaw, while on the other side of town, they kidnapped a burly porter—leader of a Bundist battle squad—and beat him to death with iron rods.

title: Goebbels visits Warsaw
summary: Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels visited Warsaw, where Pilsudski received him as the representative of a legitimate government, months after Poland signed a nonaggression pact with Germany.

citation.quote: In the summer of 1934, Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels visited Warsaw, where Pilsudski received him like the representative of any legitimate government.

title: Rothborts lose farm, buy Brooklyn house
summary: When the government seized the Rothbort family farm in 1934, Rose Rothbort used her savings to buy a house at 823 Avenue S in Brooklyn.

citation.quote: When the government finally seized their farm in 1934, she used these savings to buy a house in Brooklyn, at 823 Avenue S.

title: Sophia Dubnova turns fifty in Warsaw
summary: In 1934, Sophia Dubnova turned fifty as her eldest son Alexander returned from Berlin (after German universities expelled Jewish students) to join his brother Victor at the Free Polish University in Warsaw.

citation.quote: In 1934, Sophia Dubnova had just turned fifty, and the family was together again. German universities had expelled their Jewish students, so her eldest son, Alexander, returned from Berlin to join his brother, Victor, at the progressive Free Polish University in Warsaw.

title: Assassination of Sergei Kirov
summary: The 1934 assassination of Sergei Kirov, the closest figure Stalin had to a friend, set off the wave of purges that would consume thousands; Stalin blamed Trotsky and the old Bolshevik elite.

citation.quote: The trials sprang from the 1934 assassination of Sergei Kirov, an affable communist bureaucrat who was the closest that Stalin had to a friend.

title: Poland signs nonaggression pact with Germany
summary: Poland signed a nonaggression pact with Nazi Germany, after which the Polish government began suppressing criticism of Hitler in the Bund's press.

citation.quote: Months earlier, in January, Poland had signed a nonaggression pact with Germany.

title: Fall of Red Vienna
summary: Austrian dictator Engelbert Dollfuss attacked the Social Democrats; Schutzbund fighters barricaded inside Karl-Marx-Hof and held off government forces for three days until artillery slaughtered them along with thousands of workers.

citation.quote: In February, Austria's dictator, Engelbert Dollfuss, came for Red Vienna.

title: Founding of the Jewish Labor Committee
summary: A trio of former Bundists in New York—David Dubinsky, Baruch Charney Vladeck, and Joseph Baskin—founded the Jewish Labor Committee to help fascism's victims, representing at least 400,000 workers between them.

citation.quote: On February 25, 1934, days after the fall of Red Vienna, a trio of former Bundists in New York founded the Jewish Labor Committee to help fascism's victims, whether they were Jewish or not.

title: AFL rejects refugee quota increase
summary: At the 1935 American Federation of Labor convention, delegates from Dubinsky's union proposed a resolution to increase quotas for refugees from fascist countries, but the federation's leadership shot them down.

citation.quote: When, at the 1935 American Federation of Labor convention, delegates from Dubinsky's union proposed a resolution to increase quotas for refugees from fascist countries, the federation's leadership shot them down.

title: Poland passes new authoritarian constitution
summary: Poland passed a new constitution that eliminated the last vestiges of parliamentary democracy, making it nearly impossible for opposition parties to nominate candidates and empowering the president to appoint the prime minister and dissolve parliament at will.

citation.quote: In April 1935, Poland passed a new constitution that did away with the last vestiges of parliamentary democracy.

title: Death of Jozef Pilsudski
summary: Polish marshal Jozef Pilsudski died of stomach cancer; crowds lined his funeral cortege to the Archcathedral of Saint John, leaving power to a quartet of colonels led by Edward Rydz-Smigly.

citation.quote: He died on May 12, 1935. Crowds lined up to watch his funeral cortege pass by on the way to the Archcathedral of Saint John, where his coffin lay in state for two days, as befitted the father of modern Poland.

title: Moscow show trials of Zinoviev and Kamenev
summary: Stalin staged the Trial of the Trotskyite-Zinovievite Terrorist Center; Zinoviev, Kamenev, and other old Bolsheviks confessed to fabricated charges after torture and were shot immediately after their trial.

citation.quote: In 1936, a grandiose series of show trials rocked the convictions of the worldwide Left. The defendants were Grigori Zinoviev, Lev Kamenev, and other members of the original Bolshevik elite that had helped Lenin orchestrate the October Revolution, then construct the Soviet state.

title: Great Palestinian Revolt begins
summary: In 1936, Palestinians declared a general strike to protest the British Mandate, Jewish immigration, and unequal wages; within six months it grew into the Great Palestinian Revolt, an armed uprising against the British, Zionist institutions, and wealthy Palestinian collaborators.

citation.quote: In 1936, Palestinians declared a general strike to protest the Mandate, Jewish immigration, and the unequal wages paid to Palestinian workers. Within six months, it grew into the Great Palestinian Revolt.

title: Przytyk pogrom
summary: A pogrom broke out in Przytyk on a market day; a thousand peasants descended on Jewish stalls, hacking the shoemaker Josek apart with axes and bludgeoning his wife Chaya to death. Police arrested Jews who tried to resist.

citation.quote: On March 9, 1936, a pogrom broke out in Przytyk, a town too poor to even afford vowels.

title: Bund half-day general strike after Przytyk
summary: After the Przytyk pogrom, the Bund called a half-day general strike supported by the Polish Socialist Party; Bernard Goldstein's militia shut down Warsaw's commercial districts and the strike succeeded across Poland.

citation.quote: On March 17, just after sunrise, Bernard Goldstein's militia spread through Warsaw's commercial districts. "Shut it down," they hollered, and the traders complied.

title: Franco launches military uprising in Spain
summary: In July 1936, General Francisco Franco launched a military uprising against the elected government of Spain, beginning the first European war between socialism and fascism.

citation.quote: Ever since July 1936, when General Francisco Franco launched a military uprising against the elected government of Spain, the worldwide Left had been riveted by the peninsula.

title: Bund and Mendele the King secure Lodz election
summary: Bernard Goldstein went to Lodz where Endeks were threatening Jewish voters; with help from Jewish mob boss Mendele the King's hundreds of armed men, the Bund and Polish Socialist Party won the municipal elections.

citation.quote: In September he was in Lodz, where Endek leaflets appeared warning Jews not to vote in the next municipal election.

title: Death of Tsipie Edelman
summary: Marek Edelman's mother Tsipie died of ulcerative colitis shortly after the Bund's 1937 conference; hundreds of poor women attended her funeral.

citation.quote: His mother, Tsipie, had died of ulcerative colitis right after the Bund's 1937 conference.

title: Camp of National Unity (OZON) founded
summary: Polish Colonel Adam Koc announced OZON, a pro-government organization based on Catholicism, anti-communism, army worship, and parades; its leader called Jewish culture 'disgusting and ridiculous' and pushed for Jews to be stripped of citizenship and expelled.

citation.quote: In February 1937, top Polish politician Colonel Adam Koc announced a new pro-government organization: the Camp of National Unity, or OZON.

title: Viktor Alter visits the Spanish front
summary: In April 1937, Viktor Alter and Polish socialist Antoni Zdanowski traveled from a Paris labor conference to the Spanish front, touring Puigcerda, anarchist Barcelona, Valencia, and Madrid.

citation.quote: In April 1937, Alter was in Paris for a labor conference with his friend the Polish socialist Antoni Zdanowski. The pair decided to take a detour to the Spanish front.

title: Goldstein in Brest-Litovsk after pogrom
summary: Bernard Goldstein smuggled himself into Brest-Litovsk in May 1937, days after police had led a pogrom in the city, where he met Polish socialist Jan Dabrowski to plan defenses.

citation.quote: Bernard Goldstein smuggled himself into Brest-Litovsk in May 1937, days after police had led a pogrom in the city.

title: Attack on Bund headquarters on Dluga Street
summary: Two bullets blasted through the walls of the Bund's headquarters on Dluga Street, narrowly missing secretary Shoshke Erlich. A bomb followed, setting the foyer ablaze and injuring three Bundists and the handyman's wife.

citation.quote: On the evening of September 26, two bullets blasted through the walls of the Bund's headquarters on Dluga Street, narrowly missing the head of their secretary Shoshke Erlich.

title: Ghetto benches imposed in Polish universities
summary: In October 1937, the Polish government segregated university classrooms, forcing Jewish students to sit on the left side ('ghetto benches'). Jewish students refused, standing through lectures; the Bund and Polish socialists called a two-day general strike.

citation.quote: In October 1937, the nationalists achieved a cherished goal when the government segregated university classrooms across Poland. From then on, Jewish students would be forced to sit on the left side of the class, on so-called ghetto benches.

title: Erlich's speech at 40th anniversary of the Bund
summary: Henryk Erlich addressed three thousand people at Warsaw's Nowosci Theatre for the Bund's fortieth anniversary, denouncing nationalists, bourgeois Jewish parties, and Zionists, and calling for solidarity with the Polish working class.

citation.quote: On November 17, 1937, Henryk Erlich took the stage in Warsaw's Nowosci Theatre for the fortieth-anniversary celebration of the Bund.

title: Bund attempts Congress of Jewish Workers
summary: In the summer of 1938 the Bund tried to organize its own Congress of Jewish Workers as a counter to Zionist proposals; the Polish government quickly banned the effort.

citation.quote: In the summer of 1938, the Bund attempted to make their own competitive Congress of Jewish Workers. The Polish government soon banned their efforts.

title: Henryk Erlich warns about a Jewish state in Palestine
summary: Bundist leader Henryk Erlich wrote that a Jewish state in Palestine would face eternal fear of external Arab enemies and eternal struggle with internal Arab enemies, asking whether freedom and democracy could grow in such a climate.

citation.quote: In 1938, Henryk Erlich wrote, “If a Jewish state should arise in Palestine, its spiritual climate will be: eternal fear of the external enemy (Arabs); eternal struggle for every bit of ground with the internal enemy (Arabs)…Is this a climate in which freedom, democracy, and progress can grow? Indeed, is it not the climate in which reaction and chauvinism ordinarily flourish?”

title: Hitler annexes Austria
summary: Germany annexed Austria, sending fresh waves of Jewish refugees fleeing from both countries to closed consulates across the world.

citation.quote: Jews spilled out of Germany and Austria, which Hitler annexed in March 1938.

title: Falanga newspaper headline blames Jews for Spain
summary: A Falanga newspaper ran an April 1938 headline claiming Jews, with the help of communism and freemasonry, had murdered a hundred thousand people in Spain.

citation.quote: "Jews, with the help of communism and freemasonry, murdered a hundred thousand people in Spain," read one headline from April 1938.

title: Anti-Jewish pickets at every Jewish shop in Lodz
summary: Funded by Christian merchants' associations, picketers in April 1938 stood outside every Jewish shop in Lodz, with similar blockades organized in Volkovysk.

citation.quote: In April 1938, there were picketers outside every single Jewish shop in Lodz.

title: OZON publishes Thirteen Theses on the Jewish Question
summary: Later in May 1938, the ruling OZON party issued its Thirteen Theses, casting Jews as rootless thieves who must be forced from public life and shipped to Palestine.

citation.quote: Later that month, OZON published their pompously titled Thirteen Theses on the Jewish Question, stating that Jews were a tribe of rootless liar-thieves who needed to be forced out of jobs, universities, and public life, until the happy day when the government could finally ship them all to Palestine.

title: Nationalist bomb explodes before Bund May Day procession
summary: On May Day 1938, a nationalist bomb detonated in the main square of Warsaw's Jewish neighborhood minutes before the Bund's procession was due to pass.

citation.quote: On May Day, a nationalist bomb exploded in the main square of Warsaw's Jewish neighborhood, minutes before the Bund's procession was scheduled to pass.

title: Evian Conference on Jewish refugees
summary: President Roosevelt convened delegates from thirty-two countries at Evian-les-Bains in July 1938 to address the refugee crisis; for nine days they made excuses for refusing to admit Jews.

citation.quote: That July, President Franklin Delano Roosevelt called an international conference in the French resort town of Evian-les-Bains to figure out how the world might deal with the burden these refugees represented. Delegates from thirty-two countries attended.

title: Jacob Pat travels through Berlin
summary: In August 1938 the Bundist Jacob Pat passed through Berlin on his way home from New York, witnessing the terror of Nazi Germany and writing about it in Naye Folkstsaytung.

citation.quote: That August, the Bundist Jacob Pat passed through Berlin on his way home from New York. For a Jew, this was an act of manic daring.

title: Hitler invades Sudetenland; Munich Pact
summary: In September 1938 Hitler seized Czechoslovakia's Sudetenland with Poland grabbing borderland too; Britain and France pressured Czechoslovakia into ceding territory at Munich.

citation.quote: In September, Hitler invaded Czechoslovakia's Sudetenland, a German-majority area that contained all of the country's defensive fortifications. Poland tagged along to grab a few hundred miles of borderland for themselves.

title: Poland strips citizenship of long-absent Poles
summary: On October 6, 1938, the Polish government decreed that anyone who had lived abroad for more than five years would lose citizenship unless an embassy stamped their passport by month's end.

citation.quote: Afraid that Germany might deport Polish Jewish residents en masse, on October 6, 1938, the Polish government announced a decree that stripped the citizenship of anyone who had lived abroad for more than five years, unless the Polish embassy stamped their passports by the end of the month.

title: Lipski meets Hitler on Jewish deportations
summary: On October 21, 1938, Poland's ambassador Józef Lipski met Hitler, who proposed forcing Britain and France to grant Germany colonies where eastern European Jews could be exiled.

citation.quote: Poland's ambassador to Germany, Józef Lipski, met with Hitler on October 21. The Führer reassured him that now that the issue of Sudetenland was settled, Germany would demand France and Britain grant it colonies of its own, to which eastern Europe could exile its Jews.

title: Gestapo expels Polish Jews to Zbaszyn
summary: Beginning October 28, 1938, the Gestapo dragged sixteen thousand Polish Jews from their beds and dumped them at the border at Zbaszyn, where Polish police refused them entry.

citation.quote: On October 28, three days before the deadline set by the Polish government for Poles abroad to have their passports stamped, the Gestapo began to round up Polish Jews. They grabbed sixteen thousand people from their beds and dumped them at the border, with nothing but ten reichsmarks in their pockets and the clothes on their backs.

title: Kristallnacht pogroms across the Reich
summary: The night of Ambassador vom Rath's death, state-backed mobs across Germany, Austria, and Sudetenland torched hundreds of synagogues, destroyed thousands of businesses, and killed hundreds of Jews.

citation.quote: The night of Ambassador vom Rath's death, Nazi government unleashed a series of attacks on the Jewish population that would go down in history as Kristallnacht, the Night of Broken Glass... Around Germany, Austria, and Sudetenland, state-backed mobs torched hundreds of synagogues, destroyed thousands of businesses, and killed hundreds of Jews.

title: Erlich publishes "In the Darkest Night"
summary: A week after Kristallnacht, Henryk Erlich published an article in Naye Folkstsaytung titled "In the Darkest Night," berating Polish nationalists and the government for flirting with the Nazis.

citation.quote: A week after Kristallnacht, Henryk Erlich wrote an article titled "In the Darkest Night." In it, he berated the Polish nationalists who bayed like "jackals" to repeat Kristallnacht on their own soil, and the feckless Polish government, which flirted with the Nazis, oblivious to the fact that one day, they too might be a target.

title: Herschel Grynszpan shoots Nazi ambassador in Paris
summary: On November 7, 1938, Herschel Grynszpan—son of Zbaszyn deportees—entered the German embassy in Paris and shot the Nazi ambassador five times in the stomach.

citation.quote: On November 7, Herschel Grynszpan, the teenage son of two deportees trapped in Zbaszyn, talked his way into the German embassy in Paris. There, in the name of his countrymen, he shot the Nazi ambassador five times in the stomach.

title: Bund sweeps Polish municipal elections
summary: In the icy December 1938 municipal elections, the Bund won victories in nearly every major Jewish city in Poland, taking sixteen of nineteen Jewish seats on the Warsaw city council.

citation.quote: This love shone when the municipal elections came in December 1938. The weather was icy, but when housewives saw Bundist canvassers from their windows, they ran outside with kettles and poured them steaming glasses of tea.

title: Jews pay 40 percent of Polish taxes
summary: By 1939, Polish Jews—who made up 13 percent of the population—would pay 40 percent of the country's taxes due to discriminatory new levies on Jewish artisans.

citation.quote: The government levied new taxes on Jewish artisans; by 1939, Jews, who made up 13 percent of Poland, would pay 40 percent of the country's taxes.

title: Soviets round up Bundist activists in occupied Poland
summary: In the first weeks of World War II, the Soviets arrested hundreds of Bundist activists including Anna Rozental, YIVO director Zalman Reisen, and every Bundist on the Vilna city council.

citation.quote: In the first weeks of World War II, the Soviets rounded up hundreds of Bundist activists. The seventy-year-old leader Anna Rozental disappeared into Lukiskes, as did YIVO director Zalman Reisen, and every Bundist on the city council.

title: Bund publishes declaration in Vilna
summary: Bundist refugees in Vilna published a declaration affirming Poland as their homeland and rejecting Zionist solutions as 'wrong and utopian.'

citation.quote: That year, they published a declaration: "Poland is our homeland, where we are entitled to equal citizenship rights, where our future lies…. Any other solutions offered, under present conditions, by Zionist or other Jewish groups, are wrong and utopian, as they always were."

title: Pati Kremer writes to John Mill from Vilna
summary: In the winter of 1939, the seventy-two-year-old revolutionary Pati Kremer wrote to Bundist pioneer John Mill in New York, declaring she would remain faithful to 'our holy idea' to her final breath.

citation.quote: Pati had remained in Vilna after her husband's death. In the winter of 1939, she was seventy-two. Her health was shot, and her heart broken by her comrades' arrests, but she remained a revolutionary. She wrote to the Bundist pioneer John Mill in New York, "I believe that our holy idea will triumph, and I will remain faithful to my final breath."

title: Spanish Republic falls to Franco
summary: In February 1939 the Spanish Republic collapsed to Franco's fascists; ten thousand International Brigades fighters had died in the war, including the Warsaw Bundist Beniak Livshitz.

citation.quote: In February 1939, the Spanish Republic fell to Franco's fascists.

title: Hitler invades the rest of Czechoslovakia
summary: On March 15, 1939, Hitler invaded what remained of Czechoslovakia, sending fresh waves of refugees fleeing.

citation.quote: On March 15, Hitler invaded what was left of Czechoslovakia.

title: Hitler seizes Memel
summary: On March 23, 1939, Hitler seized Memel, a Lithuanian port city that Poland regarded as its turf, prompting Polish military mobilization.

citation.quote: On March 23, Hitler seized Memel, a Lithuanian port city that Poland regarded as its turf.

title: Hitler renounces Polish-German nonaggression pact
summary: On April 28, 1939, Hitler told the Reichstag the Polish-German nonaggression pact was "no longer in existence," to thunderous applause from the delegates.

citation.quote: On April 28, Hitler told the Reichstag that the Polish-German nonaggression pact was "no longer in existence." The delegates broke into thunderous applause.

title: Britain issues the White Paper on Palestine
summary: In May 1939 Britain issued the White Paper, promising Palestinian independence within ten years and severely curtailing Jewish immigration just as Jewish refugees most needed refuge.

citation.quote: In May, they released the White Paper, which promised an independent Palestine within ten years and severely curtailed Jewish immigration.

title: SS St. Louis departs Hamburg for Havana
summary: The same week as the British White Paper, the SS St. Louis left Hamburg for Havana with 937 Jewish refugees; Cuba admitted only 34, the US refused, and the ship was forced back to Europe.

citation.quote: The same week that the Brits announced their white paper, SS St. Louis departed from Hamburg for Havana with a cargo of 937 Jewish refugees. Each held a landing certificate for Cuba.

title: Bund May Day march of 100,000 in Warsaw
summary: At the Bund's 1939 peak, a hundred thousand people marched in their May Day parade in Warsaw; that summer they swept the next round of municipal elections.

citation.quote: Despite all this, the Bund was at its peak. In Warsaw, a hundred thousand people marched in their May Day parade. That summer, they swept the next round of municipal elections.

title: Molotov-Ribbentrop nonaggression pact signed
summary: On August 23, 1939, Nazi foreign minister Ribbentrop flew to Moscow and signed a nonaggression pact with Soviet foreign minister Molotov; Erlich denounced it in Naye Folkstsaytung.

citation.quote: On August 23, 1939, Nazi foreign minister Ribbentrop flew to Moscow, where he and the Soviet foreign minister, Vyacheslav Molotov, signed a nonaggression pact.

title: Bund proclaims readiness for supreme sacrifice
summary: In an August 29, 1939 proclamation, the Bund declared in the name of the Jewish masses their readiness to make the supreme sacrifice alongside the Polish working population.

citation.quote: "At the hour when the country's fate is to be decided," wrote the Bund in an August 29 proclamation, "we declare once more, in the name of the great Jewish masses, their readiness to make the supreme sacrifice, together with the entire working population of Poland."

title: Final Naye Folkstsaytung issue and the Warsaw trenches
summary: The August 30, 1939 final issue of Naye Folkstsaytung described a calm Warsaw and thousands of Varsovians—Bundists, nationalists, rabbis, lawyers—digging defensive trenches together around the city.

citation.quote: Warsaw was calm, the writers at Naye Folkstsaytung noted in their August 30 issue, the final one to make it abroad.

title: Volkovysk pogrom and Soviet arrival
summary: As the Polish army fled, a nationalist mob led by pharmacist Hugon Tyminski murdered seven Jews in Volkovysk, including Alexander Markov; the Red Army's arrival the next morning halted the pogrom, and Tyminski was later executed.

citation.quote: When news of the Russian invasion hit, the Polish army fled, and a mob descended on the Jewish neighborhood. They murdered seven Jews, including elderly Alexander Markov, and cheerful Itcheh, who always danced so well at weddings.

title: Haynt publishes final issue as Germany invades Poland
summary: Warsaw's Yiddish daily Haynt published its final issue the same day 1.8 million German troops crossed into Poland, striking sixty cities and routing the Polish army.

citation.quote: On September 1, Warsaw's Yiddish daily *Haynt* published its final issue. It ran a chess game, noted the mobilization of the British army, and let readers know what to consider when purchasing a gas mask.

title: German invasion of Poland begins
summary: 1.8 million German troops crossed into Poland, with bombers striking sixty cities and Panzers cutting communications, surrounding the Polish army.

citation.quote: By the time the issue was released, 1.8 million German troops had already crossed the border into Poland. Nazi bombers clouded the sky, targeting railways, and striking sixty cities at once.

title: France and Britain declare war on Germany
summary: After France and Britain declared war on Germany, Varsovians marched to the French and British embassies to honor their supposed saviors, but no help came.

citation.quote: When the two countries declared war on Germany on September 3, Varsovians marched to the French and British embassies with tricolors and union jacks to honor their saviors. No help came.

title: Arthur Zygielbojm arrives in Warsaw
summary: Bundist councilman Arthur Zygielbojm reached Warsaw on foot after a harrowing journey during which German bombers strafed his group and he was separated from his son Józef.

citation.quote: On September 8, just before midnight, Arthur Zygielbojm, a Bundist councilman from Lodz, arrived in Warsaw after a harrowing journey on foot.

title: Wehrmacht reaches Warsaw and siege begins
summary: The Wehrmacht reached Warsaw's outskirts and the city fell under siege; the next night, on the eve of Rosh Hashanah, the Luftwaffe pounded the Jewish quarter, burning twenty blocks.

citation.quote: The Wehrmacht reached Warsaw's outskirts on September 15 and the city fell under siege. The next night, on the eve of Rosh Hashanah, the Luftwaffe pounded the Jewish quarter. Twenty blocks went up in flame.

title: Erlich's group reaches Pinsk as Soviets prepare to invade
summary: After nearly 250 miles of travel, the Erlichs reached Pinsk where they heard Vyacheslav Molotov announce on the radio that Soviet troops would cross the border into Poland.

citation.quote: On the night of September 16, the Erlichs' group reached Pinsk, a pretty little market town in the northeast. At this point, Warsaw was the sole part of western Poland not in Nazi hands.

title: Soviet Union invades Poland and government flees
summary: The Red Army crossed the Polish border with ease, and that same day Poland's national government, diplomatic corps, and military leadership fled into Romania, with Marshal Rydz-Smigly leaving without final orders.

citation.quote: Due to the German invasion, few Polish soldiers remained on the Russian border, so the Red Army entered with ease. That day, the entire national government, diplomatic corps, and military leadership abandoned Poland.

title: Warsaw opposition parties meet as siege ends
summary: With no food, water, or help, Mayor Starzynski and Major General Tomaszewski convened opposition parties — excluding the Bund — to form what would become the Polish Home Army. The next day Starzynski surrendered Warsaw.

citation.quote: On September 27, the end was imminent. There was no food, no water, no help. Hitler watched the battle from across the river. Mayor Starzynski and Major General Michal Tomaszewski called a meeting of every opposition party, from the Polish Socialist Party to the Endeks.

title: Mayor Starzynski surrenders Warsaw to the Nazis
summary: Mayor Starzynski surrendered Warsaw to the Nazis; only Polish socialist leader Mek Niedzialkowski refused to sign, saying 'The working class does not capitulate.'

citation.quote: The next day Mayor Starzynski surrendered Warsaw to the Nazis. Only the Polish socialist leader Mek Niedzialkowski refused to sign. "The working class does not capitulate," he said.

title: Henryk Erlich departs Pinsk alone for Lublin
summary: Sophia hugged her husband Henryk Erlich goodbye at the Pinsk railway station as he boarded a train west toward his birthplace of Lublin, traveling alone to spare his family trouble.

citation.quote: On September 30, Sophia hugged her husband goodbye at the Pinsk railway station, and he boarded a train west, toward his birthplace.

title: Bernard Goldstein returns to a ruined Warsaw
summary: Bernard Goldstein returned to Warsaw after German bombing had leveled 10 percent of its buildings and killed forty thousand of its people.

citation.quote: When Bernard Goldstein returned to Warsaw in October, he could not believe the ruination. German bombs had leveled 10 percent of Warsaw's buildings and killed forty thousand of its people.

title: Gestapo arrests Adam Czerniakow to head the Judenrat
summary: Ten days after Warsaw's capitulation, the Gestapo arrested Adam Czerniakow and, after two days of torture, installed him as the 'elder' of the Judenrat.

citation.quote: Ten days after capitulation, the Gestapo marched into the kehillah building at 26 Grzybowska Street and arrested the interim chairman, the genteel Adam Czerniakow.

title: Bundists meet to organize the Warsaw underground
summary: Twenty Bundists, including Bernard Goldstein, Sonia Nowogrodska, Arthur Zygielbojm, Lazar Klug, and Abrasha Blum, met at a communal party kitchen to plan clandestine organizing through soup kitchens, illegal unions, and an underground political organization.

citation.quote: That October, twenty Bundists met at a communal party kitchen, with bowls of soup set in front of them as alibis. Among them were Bernard Goldstein, Sonia Nowogrodska, Arthur Zygielbojm, Lazar Klug, and Abrasha Blum.

title: Zygielbojm resigns from the Judenrat
summary: After the Gestapo ordered Warsaw's 360,000 Jews crammed into a tiny area, Arthur Zygielbojm urged the Judenrat to refuse the ghetto order. When the body refused, he resigned, knowing the consequences.

citation.quote: At the end of October, a Gestapo lieutenant stormed into the Judenrat building and ordered Adam Czerniakow, the reluctant "elder" of the Judenrat, to assemble the members and their alternates in thirty minutes, on pain of death.

title: Soviet secret police arrest Henryk Erlich at Brest-Litovsk
summary: At the Brest-Litovsk railway station, a Jewish communist identified Erlich to Soviet authorities; a secret policeman and two Red Army soldiers arrested the Bund's leader as he tried to reach Bialystok.

citation.quote: On the night of October 4, Berman and Erlich walked to the Brest-Litovsk railway station, where they hoped to catch the train to Bialystok.

title: Hitler annexes Lodz and Poznan to the Reich
summary: Hitler annexed Lodz and Poznan to the Reich, with plans for the rest of Poland to become a province for German settlers served by Polish slaves and ghettoized Jews.

citation.quote: On October 12, 1939, Hitler annexed Lodz and Poznan to the Reich. The rest of Poland would become a province, where half a million German "pioneers" could settle on dream plantations, served by Polish slaves.

title: Mayor Starzynski disappears into Gestapo custody
summary: After protesting discrimination against Jews in aid distribution at Zygielbojm's urging, Mayor Starzynski was dragged to Gestapo headquarters at Szucha Street and never seen again.

citation.quote: At Zygielbojm's urging, Mayor Starzynski protested this discrimination. On October 27, the Gestapo dragged him to their headquarters at Szucha Street. He was never seen again.

title: Soviets grant Vilna to independent Lithuania
summary: Bundists in the Soviet zone breathed a sigh of relief when the Soviets granted Vilna to independent Lithuania, allowing Shloyme Gilinsky and his family to slip across the border.

citation.quote: In November, they breathed a sigh of relief when the Soviets granted Vilna to independent Lithuania. Gilinsky and, days later, his wife and son slipped over the border past Soviet guards and their howling dogs.

title: Marek Edelman prints first issue of underground newspaper
summary: Working a hidden mimeograph machine on 67 Mila Street, Marek Edelman printed the first issue of a new monthly underground newspaper covering Nazi repressions and a future socialist Europe.

citation.quote: That November, he would print the first issue of a new monthly newspaper. It spoke about Nazi repressions of Jews and of Poles, and about the socialist and democratic Europe that would come after the present nightmare.

title: Refugees from Sierpc arrive in Warsaw
summary: Two young men arrived at the Warsaw Judenrat from Sierpc, describing how Volksdeutsche militia had herded the town's 1,700 Jews into the square, stripped and beaten them while a Polish fireman's band played a march.

citation.quote: At the start of November, two young men arrived at the Warsaw Judenrat from the tiny town of Sierpc. Their clothing was torn and bloodstained, and their faces taut with horror.

title: Medem Sanatorium reopens under Shloyme Abramson
summary: After Polish locals looted the buildings, the new director Shloyme Abramson swept up broken glass, gathered the remaining teachers, and reopened the Medem Sanatorium, which soon cared for two hundred orphans.

citation.quote: The sanatorium's new director, Shloyme Abramson, swept up the broken glass and gathered the remaining teachers, and by November the sanatorium was back in business. Soon, it cared for two hundred orphans.

title: Nazis establish ghettos across occupied Poland
summary: By the end of 1940, the Nazis had established Jewish ghettos in most towns and cities of occupied Poland, subjecting inhabitants to starvation, forced labor, and terror.

citation.quote: By the end of 1940, the Nazis had set up Jewish ghettos in most towns and cites in occupied Poland.

title: Jacob Celemenski arrives in Warsaw
summary: The Bundist courier Jacob Celemenski arrived in Warsaw in February 1940 to report on conditions in Krakow, learning the Bund's five-member cell structure and underground infrastructure.

citation.quote: He arrived in Warsaw in February 1940 to report on conditions in Krakow. Sitting in Bernard Goldstein's shabby quarters, he listened to the leaders explain their methods for organizing under the Nazi occupation.

title: Gestapo orders walls around Warsaw's Jewish neighborhood
summary: In March, the Gestapo summoned Judenrat chairman Czerniakow with a demand that the Judenrat pay for walls to encircle Warsaw's Jewish neighborhood. Twenty walls had gone up by June.

citation.quote: In March, the Gestapo summoned the Judenrat chairman Czerniakow with a demand that the Judenrat pay for walls to encircle Warsaw's Jewish neighborhood. Protection from savage Poles, the officer said.

title: Good Friday pogrom in Warsaw
summary: On Good Friday, the Nazis paid poor Polish youth four zlotys a day to attack Jewish Warsaw. Bundist labor unions formed armed battle squads with pipes and brass knuckles, fighting back for hours until the Germans called off the pogrom on the fourth day.

citation.quote: On March 22, a glittering, frosty Good Friday, the Nazis organized a tour de force of violence. They paid poor Polish youth four zlotys a day to storm Jewish Warsaw, cracking bones, breaking glass, and snatching whatever valuables they could.

title: Zygielbojm addresses Labor and Socialist International in Brussels
summary: After a brutal journey including a two-hour Gestapo whipping in Aachen, Arthur Zygielbojm arrived in Brussels and presented facts about Jewish life in Poland at the final meeting of the Labor and Socialist International, which produced only an anodyne May Day resolution.

citation.quote: On April 6, in Brussels at the last futile meeting of the Labor and Socialist International, he calmly presented facts about the life of Jews in Poland.

title: Chiune Sugihara begins issuing transit visas to Jewish refugees
summary: When Japanese vice consul Chiune Sugihara saw mobs of Jewish refugees surrounding his Kaunas embassy, he ignored Tokyo's requirements and calligraphed visas for twenty hours a day, producing papers for nearly three thousand people including 250 Bundists.

citation.quote: This understanding struck the Japanese vice consul to Lithuania, Chiune Sugihara, in June of that year, when he looked out his embassy window in Kaunas to see it surrounded by mobs of Jews.

title: Jews driven into the Warsaw ghetto
summary: For the last two weeks of October 1940, Jews dragged the remnants of their lives into the Warsaw ghetto in pouring rain, with the Bund organizing aid and protection along the way.

citation.quote: Rain pounded Warsaw for the last two weeks of October as the Jews dragged the remnants of their lives into the ghetto.

title: Nazis announce creation of the Warsaw Ghetto
summary: On Yom Kippur, loudspeakers announced the creation of a ghetto in Warsaw's Jewish neighborhood. The 113,000 Poles in the neighborhood would leave, as would 138,000 Jews and Christians of Jewish ancestry living outside it.

citation.quote: On October 12, Yom Kippur, loudspeakers announced the creation of a ghetto in Warsaw's Jewish neighborhood. The 113,000 Poles who lived in the neighborhood would leave their homes, as would 138,000 Jews and Christians of Jewish ancestry who lived outside it.

title: Gestapo executes Pole for smuggling bread into ghetto
summary: In November 1940, the Gestapo shot a Pole for smuggling a sack of bread into the Warsaw ghetto, underscoring the dangers Polish allies faced when supporting Jewish neighbors.

citation.quote: The deals were good, but even so, you can't besmirch their courage; in November, the Gestapo shot a Pole for smuggling in a sack of bread.

title: Germans seal the Warsaw ghetto gates
summary: After permitting Jews to travel to jobs in other neighborhoods for a few weeks, the Germans locked the ghetto gates on November 15, splitting Warsaw into Aryan and Jewish cities.

citation.quote: For a few weeks, the Germans permitted Jews to go to their jobs and shops in other neighborhoods, until, on November 15, they locked the gates.

title: Bund's Voice of Youth prints internationalist cover
